timeline.long_term_effect: Slightly reduces the self-harm of an Iranian closure, which is the variable that the 'threat not closure' inference depends on; the capacity is still a small fraction of Iranian exports.

timeline.name: Iran seizes two Greek tankers after a cargo confiscation
timeline.line: After the US takes an Iranian cargo from a tanker off Greece, the IRGC takes two Greek tankers in the Gulf
timeline.description: Greek authorities held a tanker carrying Iranian oil and the cargo was transferred to the United States; within weeks the IRGC seized two Greek-flagged tankers in the Gulf. Both were released in November after the cargo dispute was settled in Greek courts.
timeline.immediate_effect: Greek shipping avoided Iranian waters; insurance costs rose.
timeline.long_term_effect: The cleanest example of the seizure-for-seizure pattern: the trigger is a confiscation of Iranian cargo, the response is proportionate and reversible, and the ships come back.

timeline.name: Beijing trilateral statement restoring Saudi-Iranian relations
timeline.line: Saudi Arabia and Iran restore relations in a deal announced in Beijing, with China as guarantor
timeline.description: The two states agreed to reopen embassies within two months and reactivated their 2001 security cooperation agreement and a 1998 trade agreement. It was the first time China had brokered a security understanding between two Middle Eastern rivals.
timeline.problem_solved: Seven years of severed relations after the 2016 embassy attack, and the risk to Saudi Arabia of being the target when Iran answers US pressure.
timeline.did_it_survive: Yes so far: embassies reopened, and the relationship held through the Gaza war, the 2025 strikes and the 2026 war, in which Saudi Arabia was hit for hosting US forces and still did not join the fighting.

timeline.name: 2023 tanker seizures (Advantage Sweet, Niovi)
timeline.line: Iran seizes two tankers in a week; the US adds naval assets; traffic continues
timeline.description: Seizures followed US confiscation of Iranian oil cargoes under sanctions. The US announced additional F-35s, F-16s and a destroyer to the region in the following months.
timeline.immediate_effect: Tit-for-tat cargo seizures.
timeline.long_term_effect: Confirmed the seizure-for-seizure pattern.

timeline.name: The Houthi Red Sea campaign reroutes world shipping
timeline.line: A non-state armed group does to the Red Sea what Iran has never done to Hormuz
timeline.description: Beginning with the seizure of the Galaxy Leader in November 2023, Houthi missile and drone attacks on shipping caused most container lines to route around the Cape of Good Hope. The US announced Operation Prosperity Guardian in December 2023, and US and UK strikes followed in January 2024; traffic did not recover.
timeline.immediate_effect: War-risk premiums multiplied and Suez transits fell sharply for months.
timeline.long_term_effect: The most important comparison case in this file: it shows that durable chokepoint disruption is achievable with cheap weapons and does not require closing anything, and that escorts and strikes did not restore traffic. It also shows the limits of attributing an Iran-aligned actor's decisions to Tehran.

timeline.name: Iran seizes the St Nikolas and the MSC Aries
timeline.line: Iran takes the tanker whose cargo the US had confiscated in 2023, and then boards an Israeli-linked container ship by helicopter near the strait
timeline.description: The tanker St Nikolas, formerly the Suez Rajan, from which the US had removed Iranian oil in 2023, was seized in the Gulf of Oman in January 2024. In April, days before Iran's first direct missile strike on Israel, IRGC commandos took the MSC Aries by helicopter near the strait on the grounds of its Israeli-linked ownership.
timeline.immediate_effect: Crews detained and later released; no interruption of traffic overall.
timeline.long_term_effect: Showed the two triggers that now produce Iranian seizures: confiscation of Iranian cargo, and Israeli-linked ownership. Both remain live.

timeline.name: First direct Iran-Israel strikes
timeline.line: Iran fires drones and missiles at Israel in April and October 2024; Israel strikes Iranian air defenses
timeline.description: After Israel struck Iran's consulate in Damascus on 1 April, Iran launched roughly 300 drones and missiles on 13-14 April, mostly intercepted with US and allied help; a second, larger ballistic strike followed on 1 October after the killing of Hezbollah's leader; Israel struck Iranian air defenses and missile production on 26 October.
timeline.immediate_effect: The shadow war became direct; the strait was not affected.
timeline.long_term_effect: Set the escalation ladder that the June 2025 war climbed.

timeline.name: Russia-Iran Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty
timeline.line: Iran and Russia sign a strategic partnership that pointedly contains no mutual-defence clause
timeline.description: The treaty commits each party not to assist an aggressor against the other and to expand military-technical, energy and transport cooperation, but it does not oblige either to come to the other's defence.
timeline.problem_solved: Formalising a relationship built on drone and missile transfers and sanctions evasion.
timeline.did_it_survive: It is in force, and its limits were demonstrated in the 2025 and 2026 wars, when Russia gave Iran no military assistance.

timeline.name: NSPM-2 restores maximum pressure
timeline.line: Trump's second-term memorandum orders maximum economic pressure and denial of 'all paths to a nuclear weapon'
timeline.description: The memorandum directed Treasury to sanction all persons evidenced to be violating Iran sanctions and aimed to drive Iranian oil exports toward zero, while leaving room for talks.
timeline.immediate_effect: Enforcement against oil shipments and Chinese buyers intensified.
timeline.long_term_effect: Paired with an offer of talks, it set the pressure-plus-deadline sequence that ended in strikes in June 2025.

timeline.name: US-Iran talks mediated by Oman
timeline.line: Highest-level US-Iran nuclear talks since 2018 open in Muscat; they stall over enrichment
timeline.description: Five rounds between US envoy Steve Witkoff and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, hosted or mediated by Oman, ran from April to late May 2025. The US moved toward demanding zero enrichment; Iran refused. A sixth round scheduled for mid-June was overtaken by Israel's strikes.
timeline.immediate_effect: No agreement.
timeline.long_term_effect: Iran's reading that the talks masked a strike plan hardened its later demand for guarantees.

timeline.name: June 2025 Israel-Iran war and Majlis closure vote
timeline.line: Israel and then the US strike Iran's nuclear sites; parliament votes to close Hormuz; the strait stays open and a ceasefire follows
timeline.description: Israel opened a campaign against Iranian nuclear and military targets on 13 June; the US struck Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan on 22 June; Iran's parliament voted the same day to close the strait, a decision left to the Supreme National Security Council and not executed; Iran fired a telegraphed salvo at Al Udeid on 23 June; a ceasefire took hold on 24 June.
timeline.immediate_effect: Twelve-day war; oil rose then fell back when the strait stayed open.
timeline.long_term_effect: Even under direct attack on its nuclear program, Iran did not close the strait; the strongest data point yet for the not_implemented pattern, and also a data point for how far escalation can go without closure. Superseded in March 2026, when Iran did block the strait and then licensed passage through it: see case:2026_hormuz_closure_permit_regime. The 2025 case now reads as the last data point of the old pattern rather than as proof of it.

timeline.name: E3 snapback reimposes UN sanctions
timeline.line: Britain, France and Germany trigger snapback; pre-2016 UN sanctions return
timeline.description: The E3 notified the Security Council on 28 August 2025 of Iran's significant non-performance; after a Russia-China extension resolution failed, the UN sanctions lifted in 2016 were reinstated at the end of 27 September 2025 (New York time). Iran, Russia and China reject their validity.
timeline.immediate_effect: EU and UK reimposed their own measures within days.
timeline.long_term_effect: Ended the JCPOA's legal architecture and removed the European bridge between Washington and Tehran.

timeline.name: US executive order imposing tariffs on buyers of Iranian goods
timeline.line: Washington threatens tariffs on any country that buys Iranian goods, three weeks before the war
timeline.description: The order reaffirmed the national emergency on Iran and authorized additional tariffs on imports from countries that directly or indirectly buy Iranian goods or services.
timeline.immediate_effect: Raised costs for Iran's remaining buyers.
timeline.long_term_effect: Extended the sanctions toolkit from finance into trade policy.

timeline.name: Iran blocks Hormuz and imposes a permit-and-toll regime
timeline.line: For the first time Iran actually closes the strait, then runs it through a permit and toll authority
timeline.description: During the war Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz (late March 2026 per available accounts) and asserted authority over it. In early May it launched a 'Persian Gulf Strait Authority' requiring vessel declarations and fees before IRGC-coordinated transit. The June MOU promised 60 days of toll-free passage; at the August deadline traffic remained a small fraction of prewar levels and Iran insisted on charging fees.
timeline.immediate_effect: Collapse of commercial transits; US counter-blockade of Iranian ports reported from April.
timeline.long_term_effect: The first case in the record of an executed, sustained Hormuz disruption; it breaks the 'threat not closure' pattern once the regime itself was under direct attack.

timeline.name: Pakistan-mediated ceasefire and Islamabad talks
timeline.line: A two-week ceasefire trades a halt to strikes for reopening Hormuz; talks in Islamabad fail
timeline.description: The US and Israel agreed to pause attacks and Iran to allow coordinated passage through the strait for two weeks. Direct talks in Islamabad on 11-12 April between Vice President JD Vance and Majlis speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf did not produce a deal; reported US naval blockade of Iran followed, and the truce was violated repeatedly but extended.
timeline.immediate_effect: Reduced but did not end fighting.
timeline.long_term_effect: Made Pakistan, not Oman or Qatar, the principal channel in the war's diplomacy.

timeline.name: US-Iran Memorandum of Understanding of 17 June 2026
timeline.line: 14-point MOU halts hostilities and sets a 60-day window for a final deal on Hormuz, the nuclear program and sanctions
timeline.description: The published text declares a permanent end to military operations on all fronts including Lebanon, 60 days of toll-free passage through Hormuz with demining, downblending of enriched material under IAEA supervision, oil-sale waivers, a negotiation window of 60 days extendable by consent, and a requirement that a final deal be endorsed by a binding Security Council resolution. Sources disagree on where it was signed (Islamabad or Versailles).
timeline.problem_solved: Stopping the war and reopening the strait while deferring enrichment, missiles and sanctions to a final agreement.
timeline.did_it_survive: Partially: the 60-day window expired on 17 August 2026 without a final deal, the US rejected an extension, and the Hormuz provisions were not implemented as written; the ceasefire itself remained fragile but broadly in place.

timeline.name: MOU deadline lapses; US launches 'Operation Economic Outcast'
timeline.line: The 60-day window ends with no deal; a week later Washington announces a campaign to cut Iran's remaining economic lifelines
timeline.description: At the 17 August deadline the sides were deadlocked over control of Hormuz and nuclear talks had barely begun; Trump rejected an extension. On 24 August the White House announced 'Operation Economic Outcast' to isolate Iran financially.
timeline.immediate_effect: Return to maximum pressure without a resumption of full-scale war as of mid-September 2026.
timeline.long_term_effect: Too recent to judge.

territories.name: Abu Musa, Greater Tunb and Lesser Tunb

historical_control.note: Persian administration asserted and then displaced; the record before the twentieth century is disputed between the parties.
Britain administered the islands on behalf of the sheikhdoms of Sharjah (Abu Musa) and Ras al-Khaimah (the Tunbs).

current_claims.basis: asserts historic Persian sovereignty and treats the islands as Iranian territory; has stationed forces and civil administration on them since 1971
succeeded to the claims of Sharjah and Ras al-Khaimah; calls for direct negotiation or reference to the International Court of Justice, which Iran refuses

territories.recognition: No international body has ruled on the sovereignty question. The GCC and the Arab League restate the UAE's claim in their communiques; Russia and China have joined GCC statements calling for negotiation, drawing Iranian protests. Iran rejects any third-party adjudication.
significance: position beside the approaches to the strait
a permanent grievance that keeps the UAE aligned with outside security guarantors
the clearest case in the file of a territorial fact created by seizing an opportunity at a moment of transition

territories.name: Bahrain (the abandoned Iranian claim)

historical_control.note: Persian claims continued on paper after the Al Khalifa took the islands in 1783; effective Persian control did not.
British protected state under treaty; internal rule by the Al Khalifa.

current_claims.basis: sovereign state, UN member since 1971

territories.recognition: Universal. Iran accepted the outcome of the UN Secretary-General's 1970 survey of Bahraini opinion, which the Security Council endorsed in resolution 278; the Majlis ratified the settlement. Occasional claims by Iranian commentators and newspapers since have been disavowed by the Iranian government.
significance: the one large Iranian territorial claim in the Gulf that was dropped rather than pressed
Bahrain hosts US Naval Forces Central Command and the Fifth Fleet, which is why its status matters to the strait

territories.name: Shatt al-Arab / Arvand Rud

historical_control.note: Ottoman-Persian boundary commissions placed the river under Ottoman control with Persian rights at Khorramshahr.
The 1937 treaty kept the boundary at the low-water mark on the Iranian bank except at Abadan and Khorramshahr.
Joint: the 1975 treaty set the boundary at the thalweg, the deepest channel.

current_claims.basis: the 1975 treaty boundary at the thalweg
accepts the 1975 treaty since Saddam Hussein's letter of August 1990; Iraq had purported to abrogate it in September 1980

territories.recognition: The 1975 treaty is the instrument both states now invoke; the waterway remains silted and largely unusable for large vessels, and delimitation of the maritime boundary beyond the river mouth is unfinished.
territories.de_facto_control: shared under the 1975 treaty, with the seaward approaches patrolled by both navies and, since 2003, by coalition and Iraqi forces
significance: Iraq's only direct outlet to the Gulf, which is why an Iraqi government has twice tried to change the boundary by force
the proximate casus belli of the 1980-88 war

lessons.name: US: Gulf access is a vital interest to be defended by force
lessons.description: Stated in the 1980 State of the Union and never rescinded; the institutional expression is CENTCOM and Fifth Fleet.

lessons.name: Iran: no outside power will protect it, so build missiles and asymmetric naval forces
lessons.description: Widely attributed by analysts to the Iran-Iraq War experience of missile attacks on cities and muted international response to chemical weapons. Iranian officials invoke the war constantly, so the linkage is well supported, but the doctrine is not laid out in a single public document.

lessons.name: Iran used the strait as a threat it could not afford to execute, until it could
lessons.description: From 1984 to 2025 every Iranian closure threat went unexecuted, and the standard explanation was that Iran's own exports leave through the same water. That inference failed in 2026: with its export revenue already cut to a fraction by sanctions, its nuclear sites struck and its Supreme Leader killed, Iran blocked the strait and then imposed a permit-and-toll regime on traffic. The lesson to carry forward is the conditional, not the conclusion: the restraint held while Iran had trade to protect and a survivable alternative, and it broke when it had neither. Recorded as an inference, never as doctrine.

lessons.name: The legal status of passage through Hormuz is disputed in writing by both sides
lessons.description: UNCLOS Article 38 gives all ships and aircraft a right of transit passage that cannot be impeded or suspended, and Article 44 forbids states bordering straits from hampering it. Iran signed the convention in 1982 with a declaration that only States Parties benefit from its contractual rights, and has never ratified it; the United States has never ratified the convention either but asserts transit passage as customary law binding on Iran. Each side's position is documented, and neither has moved from it in forty years.

lessons.name: Insurance, flags and buyers stop more oil than mines or missiles
lessons.description: Every large interruption of Iranian oil in the record was produced by cutting off shipping services rather than by physical force: the British boycott of 1951-53, the EU insurance and reinsurance ban of 2012, and the shipping-focused campaign after 2018. Conversely, the fastest commercial effects of Iranian action have come through war-risk premiums rather than through damage to ships. The reading is standard in the sanctions and shipping literature; the causal weight of insurance against buyer behaviour is debated.

lessons.name: Iran runs two navies, and the one in the strait is the political one
lessons.description: US naval intelligence assessments describe a division of responsibility announced by Iran in 2007: the IRGC navy holds the Persian Gulf inside the strait with small craft, mines, anti-ship missiles and midget submarines, and the regular navy takes the Gulf of Oman and beyond. Seizures and harassment inside the Gulf are therefore IRGC decisions, which matters when judging whether an incident reflects national policy or a service acting on standing authority.

lessons.name: Disruption of the strait is a dial, and in 2026 Iran found the setting that pays
lessons.description: The debate before 2026 was posed as closure or no closure. What happened instead was a blockade during the war followed by a permit-and-toll authority that lets traffic through on Iranian terms. That is a form of disruption that earns revenue and asserts sovereignty rather than destroying Iran's own export route, which is exactly what the older 'Iran cannot afford to close it' inference failed to anticipate. This is an inference from one recent case, not doctrine, and it may not survive the settlement of the current standoff.

tendencies.name: Iran retaliates in ways that are visible, deniable or telegraphed, and stop short of war with the US
contradicting: The 1984-88 Tanker War escalated to direct US-Iran naval combat; the 2019 Abqaiq attack, if Iranian, was a major unclaimed strike on a US partner; the October 2024 salvo was larger and less telegraphed than April's.

The 2026 war broke the pattern at both ends: Iran's retaliation for the strikes that killed Ali Khamenei included attacks on Gulf states hosting US forces and an actual blockade of the strait, neither of which is calibrated in the sense the earlier cases were.
current_evidence: The June 2025 Al Udeid strike was announced in advance through Qatar and caused no casualties.
Under Mojtaba Khamenei the record is six months long and wartime; the April 2026 ceasefire and the June MOU were accepted while the toll regime was kept in place.
tendencies.caveat: Calibration held while the regime's survival was not at stake and while Ali Khamenei was making the decisions. Both conditions failed in 2026. Any use of this tendency now has to say which leadership it describes.

tendencies.name: Iran answers a seizure of its cargo with a seizure of someone else's, and gives the ships back
contradicting: The 2026 permit regime was not a seizure answering a seizure but a general assertion of control over all traffic, which breaks the proportional, reversible form.
Many US confiscations of Iranian cargo produced no Iranian seizure at all, so the response is selective rather than automatic.
current_evidence: The January 2024 seizure of the St Nikolas took the very tanker whose Iranian cargo the United States had confiscated in 2023.
tendencies.caveat: The pattern describes IRGC behaviour in peacetime pressure, not in war. It held for seventeen years and then did not describe 2026 at all. Crews have been released in every case, but detentions have lasted months.

tendencies.name: Washington's first answer to threatened shipping is to escort it, not to strike the source
current_evidence: In 2019 the US called off a retaliatory strike after its drone was shot down and stood up an escort coalition instead; in 2023-24 it answered Red Sea attacks with a task force first and strikes second.
tendencies.caveat: The preference has been reversed whenever US personnel were killed or a US ship was hit, and it was abandoned entirely in 2025-26. Escorting is the default, not a rule, and the 2026 record shows what happens when the default is dropped.

tendencies.name: The Arab Gulf states host the American forces and then insure themselves against the war those forces might start
contradicting: The 1980s: Saudi Arabia and Kuwait financed Iraq's war against Iran and Kuwait asked for superpower protection outright.
Bahrain and the UAE signed the Abraham Accords in 2020 and Bahrain a US security agreement in 2023, both of which align rather than hedge.
current_evidence: Saudi Arabia and Qatar were struck in 2025 and 2026 for hosting US forces and neither joined the war; both kept channels to Tehran open throughout.
tendencies.caveat: Hedging is what small exposed states do when they judge the threat to be survivable. A direct attack on a ruling family or on the oil complex itself has never been tested, and the Kuwaiti precedent of 1987 shows the same states will ask for open protection when the threat is existential.

path_dependencies.name: From 1979 to export dependence on China through the same strait

chain.step: 1979 revolution and hostage crisis break US-Iran relations
Sanctions regimes accumulate (1979, 1995, 2006-10 UN, 2012 EU, 2018 US)
Iran's oil exports narrow to a small set of buyers, mostly China, shipped through Hormuz
Current constraint: closing the strait would cut Iran's main revenue; threatening it remains cheap

path_dependencies.description: Documented sanctions and trade data; the constraint on Iranian behaviour is an assessment.

path_dependencies.name: From a British budget decision in 1968 to the Gulf's longest territorial dispute

chain.step: January 1968: Britain announces it will leave the Gulf by the end of 1971
May 1970: Iran trades its claim to Bahrain for a UN-endorsed settlement, clearing the way for the smaller states' independence
30 November 1971: with protection lapsing the next day, Iran takes Abu Musa and the Tunbs
2 December 1971: the UAE is founded and inherits the claim it cannot enforce
Current constraint: Iranian forces sit on islands beside the approaches; the UAE restates its claim annually and keeps outside security guarantors; Iran refuses adjudication

path_dependencies.description: The documents and dates are firm. The arrow from the withdrawal announcement to the seizure is an assessment: the Shah had pressed the claim earlier, and a different British handover, or a different ruler in Tehran, might have produced a negotiated outcome as Bahrain's did.

path_dependencies.name: From cutting Iran out of shipping to Iran charging for shipping

chain.step: 1951-53: Britain shows that Iranian oil can be stopped by denying buyers, hulls and insurance rather than by blockade
2012: the EU bans insurance and reinsurance of Iranian cargoes and Iranian exports roughly halve
2018 onward: maximum pressure targets tankers, masters and buyers; Iran builds a dark fleet and sells almost exclusively to China
2021: Iran opens its own small bypass at Jask, reducing but not removing its dependence on the strait
2026: under attack and with little export revenue left to protect, Iran blocks the strait and then licenses and taxes passage through it
Current constraint: the cost of closure to Iran falls as its own trade through the strait falls, so the restraint that held from 1984 to 2025 is weaker than the historical record alone suggests

path_dependencies.description: Each step is documented. The final arrow is the important hypothesis and it cuts against the older reading in this file: a state with less to lose at sea is cheaper to deter in theory and harder to deter in practice. Competing reading: the 2026 regime was a wartime improvisation that will disappear with a settlement, not a new equilibrium.

narratives.name: Iran: a century of foreign interference justifies resistance and self-reliance
narratives.historical_event: 1953 coup; 1980-88 war; sanctions
narratives.modern_interpretation: The Islamic Republic frames its foreign policy as resistance to US and Israeli domination. The 1953 coup is documented; the claim that current US policy continues it is a political interpretation.

narratives.name: US: Iran as a hostage-taking, terror-sponsoring regime since 1979
narratives.historical_event: 1979-81 embassy seizure; 1983 Beirut bombings
narratives.modern_interpretation: Frames US policy across administrations and constrains any president's room to normalize relations. The events are documented; the framing is a domestic political narrative.

narratives.name: The name of the Gulf as a sovereignty claim on both shores
narratives.historical_event: Persian naming of the Gulf in classical and early modern usage, and the Safavid recapture of Hormuz from Portugal in 1622.
narratives.modern_interpretation: Iran treats 'Persian Gulf' as a matter of sovereignty and history, marks a National Persian Gulf Day tied to the 1622 anniversary, and has protested against airlines, publishers and foreign officials who use 'Arabian Gulf'. Gulf Arab states use 'Arabian Gulf' as standard: a former editor of Abu Dhabi's The National has described an outright ban on the Persian form. The dispute is documented on both sides; the claim that a name settles a sovereignty question is not.
used_in: Iranian official statements and annual commemoration
protests over foreign government and airline usage

narratives.name: Iran: the airliner the Americans shot down and never apologised for
narratives.historical_event: The destruction of Iran Air flight 655 by USS Vincennes on 3 July 1988, killing 290 people; a 1996 settlement paid compensation without an apology.
narratives.modern_interpretation: Iranian officials and state media present the shoot-down as deliberate or at least as proof of American indifference to Iranian life, and invoke it whenever US force in the Gulf is discussed. The United States has always maintained it was a mistake by a crew that believed it was under attack. The facts of the killing and the compensation are settled; the intent is not, and the file records both readings.
used_in: Iranian responses to criticism over the 2020 shoot-down of flight PS752

narratives.name: Gulf Arab states: a revolutionary neighbour that takes what it can
narratives.historical_event: The 1971 seizure of Abu Musa and the Tunbs, the Iranian claim to Bahrain before 1970, the export of the revolution after 1979, and the 1981 and 1996 plots and bombings attributed to Iranian-linked networks in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia.
narratives.modern_interpretation: GCC communiques restate the islands claim at every summit and frame Iranian regional policy as expansion under religious cover. The islands seizure and the attributed attacks are documented; the reading of every Iranian action as one campaign is a political frame, and it coexists with the same governments' trade with Iran and, since 2023, restored relations.
used_in: GCC and Arab League summit communiques
UAE statements at the UN General Assembly

cases.name: Egyptian mobilization into Sinai, May 1967
Egyptian and Syrian mobilization under exercise cover, October 1973
Exercise Brasstacks crisis
1990 Kashmir crisis
Iraqi buildup on the Kuwaiti border, July 1990
India's Operation Parakram
Russia-Georgia war
Seizure of Crimea and outbreak of the Donbas war
Doklam standoff
Russian spring 2021 buildup on Ukraine's border
Winter 2021-22 buildup and full-scale invasion

pooled.note: n=11; pooling moves it 42% toward the parent distribution over 101 classed cases.

border_mobilization.selection_note: Cases are large, visible troop concentrations on a neighbour's border. The set is drawn from well-documented crises and is biased toward mobilizations that became famous because they led to war; quiet buildups that dissolved are under-recorded. Treat the war share as an upper bound on the prior, not a point estimate.

cases.name: Tanker War
Iran seizes fifteen Royal Navy personnel
IRGC fast boats swarm US warships in the strait
Closure threats during the 2011-12 sanctions escalation
Iran seizes the Maersk Tigris in the strait
Ten US sailors detained at Farsi Island
Closure threats after the US withdrawal from the nuclear deal
2019 tanker attacks, drone shoot-down and seizures
Iran seizes two Greek tankers after a cargo confiscation
2023 tanker seizures (Advantage Sweet, Niovi)
Iran seizes the St Nikolas and the MSC Aries
June 2025 Israel-Iran war and Majlis closure vote
Iran blocks Hormuz and imposes a permit-and-toll regime

pooled.note: n=13; pooling moves it 38% toward the parent distribution over 101 classed cases.

hormuz_disruption.selection_note: Cases are episodes in which Iran threatened, attacked, boarded or seized shipping or naval personnel in or near the Strait of Hormuz, or acted to control passage through it. Coding: 'not_implemented' means a closure threat was made and not acted on; 'limited_conflict' means attacks or seizures occurred without closure; 'de_escalation' means an incident ended within days with the people or ship returned and no further action; 'prolonged_standoff' is used for the 2026 blockade and permit regime, which is still running. The set is assembled from publicised incidents, so it over-represents episodes that governments wanted known and under-represents routine harassment, near-misses and the many US cargo confiscations that drew no Iranian response. The 1984-88 Tanker War is counted once although it contains hundreds of attacks, which understates how violent that period was relative to the single-incident cases. Most importantly, the set is not a sample of independent draws: eleven of the cases fall under Ali Khamenei's leadership and one under his successor's, and the first executed disruption in the whole record came in 2026, after the strikes on Iran's nuclear programme and his death. A base rate built on the pre-2026 cases would have said closure does not happen; it happened. Use the distribution as a prior about peacetime pressure and discard it for wartime.

why_it_matters.name: Balfour Declaration
why_it_matters.line: Britain backs 'a national home for the Jewish people' in Palestine

why_it_matters.name: 1947-49 Palestine War (Israel's War of Independence; the Nakba)
why_it_matters.line: Civil war and Arab invasion end with Israel established, Palestine divided and some 700,000 Palestinians displaced

why_it_matters.name: Six-Day War (June 1967)
why_it_matters.line: In six days Israel takes the West Bank, East Jerusalem, Gaza, Sinai and the Golan

why_it_matters.name: UN Security Council Resolution 242
why_it_matters.line: Resolution 242 sets the 'land for peace' formula every later peace deal builds on

why_it_matters.name: Oslo I: Declaration of Principles
why_it_matters.line: Israel and the PLO recognize each other and agree interim self-rule, deferring every hard issue

why_it_matters.name: Hamas wins elections, seizes Gaza; blockade imposed
why_it_matters.line: Hamas wins the 2006 legislative election and in 2007 seizes Gaza; Israel and Egypt close it off

why_it_matters.name: Nation-State Law
why_it_matters.line: Israel constitutionally defines itself as the nation state of the Jewish people

why_it_matters.name: Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, 7 October 2023
why_it_matters.line: Hamas breaks through the Gaza fence, kills about 1,200 people in Israel and takes 251 hostages

why_it_matters.name: October 2025 Gaza ceasefire under the 20-point plan
why_it_matters.line: Hamas returns the living hostages and Israel pulls back to a 'yellow line' under Trump's 20-point plan; disarmament and governance are left for later

timeline.name: Hussein-McMahon correspondence
timeline.line: Britain promises Arab independence for a revolt against the Ottomans, with disputed exclusions
timeline.description: Britain's High Commissioner in Egypt promised to support Arab independence in return for a revolt against the Ottomans, excluding areas 'lying to the west of the districts of Damascus, Homs, Hama and Aleppo'. Whether Palestine was excluded is contested: British governments said yes; Arab leaders and some historians say no.
timeline.immediate_effect: Arab Revolt of 1916.
timeline.long_term_effect: Basis of the Arab argument that Britain made incompatible promises (with Sykes-Picot and Balfour).

timeline.name: Sykes-Picot Agreement
timeline.line: Britain and France secretly divide the Ottoman Arab provinces
timeline.description: Secret Anglo-French agreement dividing Ottoman Arab lands into zones of control and influence, with Palestine marked for an international administration.
timeline.immediate_effect: Framework for the post-war mandates.
timeline.long_term_effect: Invoked in Arab narratives of Western betrayal; the Syria-Lebanon/Palestine-Transjordan split that followed shaped today's state borders.

timeline.name: Balfour Declaration
timeline.line: Britain backs 'a national home for the Jewish people' in Palestine
timeline.description: The British government declared support for a Jewish national home in Palestine, provided nothing prejudiced the civil and religious rights of 'existing non-Jewish communities', who were then the large majority.
timeline.immediate_effect: British policy commitment weeks before the capture of Jerusalem.
timeline.long_term_effect: Written into the 1922 Mandate; the founding document of the dispute for both sides: legitimation for Zionists, dispossession for Palestinians.

timeline.name: League of Nations Mandate for Palestine
timeline.line: League of Nations entrusts Palestine to Britain with the Balfour pledge built in
timeline.description: The Mandate incorporated the Balfour Declaration, recognized a Jewish agency and required facilitating Jewish immigration; Article 25 let Britain exclude Transjordan from those provisions, which it did.
timeline.immediate_effect: Separate Palestine and Transjordan administrations; legal framework for immigration.
timeline.long_term_effect: Set the outer boundaries later contested between Israel, Jordan, Egypt and the Palestinians; Mandate law survives in Israeli, Jordanian and PA legal systems.

timeline.name: 1929 riots over the Western Wall
timeline.line: A dispute over prayer at the Western Wall turns into riots; Hebron's Jewish community is destroyed
timeline.description: Tension over Jewish worship arrangements at the Western Wall led to Arab riots; 133 Jews and 116 Arabs were killed, including a massacre in Hebron. The Shaw Commission blamed Arab fears of Jewish immigration and land purchase.
timeline.immediate_effect: Hebron's old Jewish community evacuated; British inquiries into immigration.
timeline.long_term_effect: First large instance of the holy-site trigger; Jewish self-defence organization (Haganah) expanded.

timeline.name: Peel Commission proposes partition
timeline.line: During the Arab Revolt, a British commission first proposes partitioning Palestine
timeline.description: Responding to the 1936-39 Arab Revolt, the Peel Commission judged the Mandate unworkable and proposed a small Jewish state, an Arab state joined to Transjordan, and a British zone including Jerusalem, with population transfer.
timeline.immediate_effect: Rejected by the Arab Higher Committee; Zionist leadership accepted the principle while disputing the borders.
timeline.long_term_effect: Introduced partition as the default international solution.

timeline.name: MacDonald White Paper
timeline.line: Britain caps Jewish immigration at 75,000 over five years on the eve of the Holocaust
timeline.description: Abandoned partition, capped Jewish immigration at 75,000 over five years (further immigration subject to Arab consent), restricted land sales and envisaged an independent state within ten years.
timeline.immediate_effect: Zionist break with Britain; illegal immigration and, after 1944, armed Jewish revolt against British rule.
timeline.long_term_effect: Britain's inability to hold either community led it to hand the question to the UN in 1947.

timeline.name: UN General Assembly Resolution 181 (partition plan)
timeline.line: UN recommends partition into Jewish and Arab states with an international Jerusalem
timeline.description: Recommended independent Jewish and Arab states in economic union and an internationally administered Jerusalem. The Jewish Agency accepted; the Arab Higher Committee and Arab states rejected it as a violation of majority self-determination.
timeline.immediate_effect: Civil war in Palestine began the next day.
timeline.long_term_effect: Cited by Israel's Declaration of Independence and by the 1988 Palestinian declaration alike as international legitimacy for statehood; the source of the corpus separatum position many states still hold on Jerusalem.

timeline.name: Displacement of Palestinian Arabs, 1947-49
timeline.line: Some 700,000-750,000 Palestinian Arabs flee or are expelled and are not allowed to return
timeline.description: Roughly 700,000-750,000 Arabs left or were driven from territory that became Israel, and hundreds of villages were depopulated; Israel barred their return. The scale is broadly agreed; the causes are contested: archival historians such as Morris describe a mix of expulsions, flight from fighting and fear without a single master plan, while Palestinian historians and scholars such as Pappe argue for systematic expulsion.
timeline.immediate_effect: Arab minority of about 150,000 remained inside Israel; refugee camps in Gaza, the West Bank, Jordan, Lebanon and Syria.
timeline.long_term_effect: The 'right of return' became a core Palestinian demand and a red line for Israel, which sees it as ending the Jewish majority.

timeline.name: Declaration of the State of Israel
timeline.line: Israel declares independence as the Mandate ends; the US recognizes it within minutes
timeline.description: The Provisional State Council declared a Jewish state in Eretz-Israel citing historical right and UNGA 181; the United States extended de facto recognition the same day and the USSR de jure recognition three days later.
timeline.immediate_effect: Arab state armies entered Palestine on 15 May.
timeline.long_term_effect: The declaration defines Israel as a Jewish state promising equal rights to all inhabitants, a pairing still litigated in Israeli politics (see the 2018 Nation-State Law).

timeline.name: 1947-49 Palestine War (Israel's War of Independence; the Nakba)
timeline.line: Civil war and Arab invasion end with Israel established, Palestine divided and some 700,000 Palestinians displaced
timeline.description: A civil war between Jewish and Arab forces (November 1947-May 1948) was followed by the intervention of Arab state armies after Israel declared independence. Israel ended the war holding about 78 percent of Mandatory Palestine; Jordan held the West Bank and East Jerusalem, Egypt the Gaza Strip.
timeline.immediate_effect: Israel established; no Palestinian Arab state; a mass refugee population.
timeline.long_term_effect: The 1949 armistice lines (Green Line) became the '1967 borders' of later diplomacy; refugees and their descendants remain a final-status issue.

timeline.name: UN General Assembly Resolution 194, paragraph 11
timeline.line: UN resolves that refugees wishing to return and live at peace should be permitted to
timeline.description: Paragraph 11 resolved that refugees wishing to return to their homes and live at peace with their neighbours should be permitted to do so at the earliest practicable date, with compensation for those choosing not to return.
timeline.immediate_effect: No implementation.
timeline.long_term_effect: The legal anchor Palestinians cite for the right of return; Israel reads it as a non-binding recommendation conditioned on peace.

timeline.name: 1949 Armistice Agreements (Rhodes and others)
timeline.line: Armistices with Egypt, Lebanon, Jordan and Syria draw the Green Line
timeline.description: Four UN-mediated agreements (Egypt February, Lebanon March, Jordan April, Syria July 1949) set demarcation lines that the texts said were military, not political, boundaries.
timeline.problem_solved: Ending interstate fighting of the 1948 war.
timeline.did_it_survive: The lines held with violations until the 1967 war; they survive as the reference line ('1967 borders') of UNSCR 242 diplomacy, UNSCR 2334 and the Arab Peace Initiative.

timeline.name: UNRWA established
timeline.line: UN creates a dedicated agency for Palestinian refugees that registers their descendants
timeline.description: UNGA 302 (IV) created UNRWA to provide relief and works for Palestine refugees; it began operations in May 1950 and registers descendants of male refugees as refugees.
timeline.immediate_effect: Schools, clinics and rations in camps across five fields.
timeline.long_term_effect: Kept refugee status institutionalized across generations, which Israel calls an obstacle to settlement and Palestinians call a guarantee of the right of return; Israel legislated against UNRWA in 2024.

timeline.name: Jordan annexes the West Bank and East Jerusalem
timeline.line: Jordan formally annexes the West Bank, recognized by almost no one
timeline.description: Jordan's parliament approved union of the two banks; the Arab League objected and almost no states recognized it. Palestinians in the West Bank received Jordanian citizenship.
timeline.immediate_effect: West Bank ruled from Amman until 1967.
timeline.long_term_effect: Jordan's claim lasted until the 1988 disengagement; Jordan's custodial role at Jerusalem's Muslim shrines survives.

timeline.name: Israel's Law of Return
timeline.line: Every Jew gains the right to immigrate to Israel
timeline.description: Granted every Jew the right to immigrate and, with the 1952 Citizenship Law, citizenship; amended in 1970 to include children and grandchildren of Jews.
timeline.immediate_effect: Mass immigration, including from Arab countries, roughly doubled Israel's Jewish population within a few years.
timeline.long_term_effect: Demography is linked to the conflict's final-status positions: the Jewish-majority rationale underlies Israel's rejection of a Palestinian right of return.

timeline.name: Suez Crisis / Sinai Campaign
timeline.line: Israel invades Sinai in collusion with Britain and France, then withdraws under US pressure
timeline.description: After Egypt nationalized the Suez Canal Company, Israel invaded Sinai on 29 October in coordination with Britain and France. US pressure forced a ceasefire and Israeli withdrawal by March 1957; a UN Emergency Force deployed in Sinai and Israel gained shipping through the Straits of Tiran.
timeline.immediate_effect: Israeli withdrawal; UNEF on the Egyptian side.
timeline.long_term_effect: The removal of UNEF and closure of Tiran in May 1967 recreated the pre-1956 situation and helped trigger the 1967 war.

timeline.name: PLO founded
timeline.line: Arab League creates the PLO; Fatah takes it over after 1967
timeline.description: The Palestine National Council met in East Jerusalem under Arab League sponsorship. After the 1967 defeat, guerrilla factions led by Fatah took control and Yasser Arafat became chairman in 1969; the 1968 Charter declared armed struggle 'the only way to liberate Palestine'.
timeline.immediate_effect: A Palestinian national institution separate from the Arab states.
timeline.long_term_effect: The PLO signed Oslo and remains the party that negotiates for Palestinians internationally.

timeline.name: Egyptian mobilization into Sinai, May 1967
timeline.description: Egypt moved forces into Sinai, expelled UNEF and closed the Straits of Tiran; Israel struck first on 5 June.

timeline.name: Six-Day War (June 1967)
timeline.line: In six days Israel takes the West Bank, East Jerusalem, Gaza, Sinai and the Golan
timeline.description: Israel's pre-emptive air strike on Egypt opened a war in which it captured Sinai and Gaza from Egypt, the West Bank and East Jerusalem from Jordan, and the Golan Heights from Syria. Several hundred thousand Palestinians were displaced, many for the second time.
timeline.immediate_effect: Israeli military rule over about a million Palestinians; Jerusalem unified under Israeli control.
timeline.long_term_effect: Created the occupation, the settlement enterprise and the 'land for peace' formula; every later negotiation is about the 1967 territories.

timeline.name: Khartoum Arab Summit: 'the three noes'
timeline.line: Arab states pledge no peace, no recognition and no negotiation with Israel
timeline.description: Paragraph 3 committed Arab states to 'no peace with Israel, no recognition of Israel, no negotiations with it'. Some historians argue Nasser and Hussein used it as cover for indirect diplomacy, so its practical meaning is debated.
timeline.immediate_effect: Israel's post-war offers of withdrawal for peace went unanswered.
timeline.long_term_effect: Invoked by Israelis as proof of Arab rejectionism; reversed by the 2002 Arab Peace Initiative.

timeline.name: UN Security Council Resolution 242
timeline.line: Resolution 242 sets the 'land for peace' formula every later peace deal builds on
timeline.description: Called for 'withdrawal of Israeli armed forces from territories occupied in the recent conflict' and for every state's right to live in peace within secure and recognized boundaries. It refers to refugees but not to Palestinians as a people. Its English text omits 'the' before 'territories'; Israel and the US read that as not requiring full withdrawal, Arab states read it (and the French text) as requiring full withdrawal.
timeline.immediate_effect: Accepted by Egypt, Jordan and Israel; rejected by Syria and the PLO until later.
timeline.long_term_effect: Named as the basis of Camp David, the 1979 and 1994 treaties, Madrid and Oslo.

timeline.name: Black September: Jordan expels the PLO
timeline.line: Jordan's army crushes Palestinian guerrillas, pushing the PLO to Lebanon
timeline.description: After PLO factions hijacked airliners and challenged the monarchy, the Jordanian army attacked guerrilla bases; a Syrian armoured incursion was repulsed. The PLO leadership relocated to Lebanon by 1971.
timeline.immediate_effect: PLO base moved to Lebanon.
timeline.long_term_effect: Destabilized Lebanon and set up the 1982 Israeli invasion; a precedent that Arab states would fight the PLO to protect their own regimes.

timeline.name: Egyptian and Syrian mobilization under exercise cover, October 1973
timeline.description: Repeated exercises had desensitized Israeli intelligence; the real attack came on 6 October.

timeline.name: October 1973 War (Yom Kippur / Ramadan War)
timeline.line: Egypt and Syria surprise Israel; Israel recovers militarily but the shock opens the road to peace with Egypt
timeline.description: Egypt and Syria attacked on Yom Kippur; Israel was surprised because its intelligence 'conception' held that Egypt would not attack without air superiority. Israel reversed early losses; a superpower confrontation and Arab oil embargo followed; UNSCR 338 called for a ceasefire and negotiations.
timeline.immediate_effect: Agranat Commission; Prime Minister Meir resigned in 1974; Kissinger's disengagement agreements.
timeline.long_term_effect: Restored Egyptian standing enough for Sadat to negotiate, leading to Camp David; the intelligence failure became the reference point for 7 October 2023.

timeline.name: Rabat summit and UN observer status for the PLO
timeline.line: Arab states name the PLO the Palestinians' sole legitimate representative; the UN grants it observer status
timeline.description: The Rabat Arab summit named the PLO the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people, over Jordan's objections; Arafat addressed the UN General Assembly, which affirmed Palestinian self-determination (3236) and gave the PLO observer status (3237).
timeline.immediate_effect: Jordan sidelined as spokesman for the West Bank.
timeline.long_term_effect: Made the PLO the unavoidable interlocutor, which Israel accepted only in 1993.

timeline.name: Camp David Accords
timeline.line: Carter, Sadat and Begin agree a framework for Egyptian-Israeli peace and Palestinian autonomy
timeline.description: Two frameworks: one for an Egyptian-Israeli treaty, one for a five-year transitional self-governing authority in the West Bank and Gaza followed by final-status talks. The PLO and Jordan were not party.
timeline.problem_solved: Separating Egyptian peace from the Palestinian question.
timeline.did_it_survive: The Egypt framework became the 1979 treaty; the Palestinian autonomy framework was never implemented, though its five-year interim model reappeared in Oslo.

timeline.name: Egypt-Israel Peace Treaty
timeline.line: Egypt becomes the first Arab state to make peace with Israel, regaining all of Sinai
timeline.description: Israel withdrew from Sinai in stages to April 1982 and dismantled its settlements there; Egypt recognized Israel and opened diplomatic relations; a Multinational Force and Observers verifies limits on forces.
timeline.problem_solved: Ending war between Israel and the largest Arab army.
timeline.did_it_survive: Yes: through Sadat's assassination (1981), the Lebanon wars, both intifadas, the Muslim Brotherhood presidency (2012-13) and the 2023-25 Gaza war, though as a 'cold peace'. Egypt was suspended from the Arab League 1979-1989.

timeline.name: Basic Law: Jerusalem, Capital of Israel
timeline.line: Israel declares 'complete and united' Jerusalem its capital; the UN calls the law null and void
timeline.description: Constitutionalized the 1967 extension of Israeli law to East Jerusalem. UNSCR 478 declared it null and void and called on states to withdraw embassies from the city, which most did.
timeline.immediate_effect: Embassies moved to Tel Aviv.
timeline.long_term_effect: The formal annexation that the 2017 US recognition partly accepted and the PA and most states reject.

timeline.name: Golan Heights Law
timeline.line: Israel extends its law to the Golan; the UN rejects it; the US recognizes it in 2019
timeline.description: Applied Israeli law, jurisdiction and administration to the Golan Heights; UNSCR 497 declared it null and void. The United States recognized Israeli sovereignty in March 2019.
timeline.immediate_effect: De facto annexation.
timeline.long_term_effect: Removed the Golan from the land-for-peace formula in Israeli domestic politics; Israel-Syria talks in the 1990s-2000s nonetheless discussed withdrawal.

timeline.name: 1982 Lebanon War and occupation of south Lebanon
timeline.line: Israel invades Lebanon to expel the PLO, which leaves for Tunis; Hezbollah rises during the 18-year occupation
timeline.description: Israel invaded to destroy the PLO's base, besieged Beirut and forced the PLO's evacuation to Tunis in August 1982. In September, Lebanese Phalangist militiamen massacred civilians in Sabra and Shatila; Israel's Kahan Commission found Defense Minister Sharon bore personal responsibility. Israel held a southern 'security zone' until withdrawing in May 2000.
timeline.immediate_effect: PLO dispersed; Sharon resigned as defense minister.
timeline.long_term_effect: Iran-backed Hezbollah formed during the occupation and became Israel's most capable non-state adversary; the unilateral 2000 withdrawal shaped later Israeli debates.

timeline.name: First Intifada and the founding of Hamas
timeline.line: A popular uprising in the territories begins; the Muslim Brotherhood launches Hamas
timeline.description: Mass protests, strikes and stone-throwing spread from Gaza to the West Bank. The Gaza Muslim Brotherhood founded Hamas in December 1987; its August 1988 Covenant called for Islamic rule over all of Palestine and rejected negotiated settlement.
timeline.immediate_effect: Shifted Palestinian politics from the exile PLO to the territories; Jordan disengaged in 1988.
timeline.long_term_effect: Created the Islamist rival to the PLO that later won elections and took Gaza; convinced Israeli leaders that occupation had costs, opening the way to Madrid and Oslo.

timeline.name: Jordanian disengagement and the Palestinian Declaration of Independence
timeline.line: Jordan drops its West Bank claim; the PLO declares a State of Palestine and implicitly accepts two states
timeline.description: King Hussein severed legal and administrative ties with the West Bank on 31 July 1988. The PNC in Algiers declared the State of Palestine on 15 November, citing UNGA 181 and accepting UNSCR 242; in December Arafat renounced terrorism and the US opened a dialogue with the PLO.
timeline.immediate_effect: Dozens of states recognized Palestine; the PLO's shift to a two-state position.
timeline.long_term_effect: The PLO's claim narrowed to the 1967 territories; the basis for Oslo mutual recognition.

timeline.name: Madrid Peace Conference
timeline.line: After the Gulf War, the US convenes the first direct talks between Israel and its Arab neighbours
timeline.description: US and Soviet co-sponsored conference launched bilateral tracks between Israel and Syria, Lebanon and a joint Jordanian-Palestinian delegation (PLO excluded formally), on the basis of UNSCR 242 and 338.
timeline.immediate_effect: Bilateral talks in Washington that stalled.
timeline.long_term_effect: The official track was overtaken by secret Israel-PLO talks in Oslo; the Jordan track produced the 1994 treaty.

timeline.name: Oslo I: Declaration of Principles
timeline.line: Israel and the PLO recognize each other and agree interim self-rule, deferring every hard issue
timeline.description: Preceded by letters of mutual recognition (9 September), the Declaration created a five-year interim period of Palestinian self-government and deferred Jerusalem, refugees, settlements, security arrangements and borders to permanent status negotiations (Article V).
timeline.problem_solved: Mutual recognition and a phased process when final-status gaps were unbridgeable.
timeline.did_it_survive: Partly: the PA and the Israel-PLO recognition survive, but the permanent-status deadline (1999) passed without agreement, and the interim arrangements became semi-permanent.

timeline.name: Israel-Jordan Peace Treaty (Wadi Araba)
timeline.line: Jordan makes peace with Israel; Israel acknowledges Jordan's special role at Jerusalem's Muslim shrines
timeline.description: Fixed the international boundary, included water-sharing provisions, and in Article 9 committed Israel to respect Jordan's 'present special role' in Muslim holy shrines in Jerusalem.
timeline.problem_solved: Formalizing a long de facto relationship once the PLO had signed Oslo.
timeline.did_it_survive: Yes, through both intifadas and the Gaza wars, though Jordan recalled its ambassador in November 2023 and relations are strained over Al-Aqsa.

timeline.name: Oslo II: Interim Agreement on the West Bank and Gaza
timeline.line: Oslo II divides the West Bank into Areas A, B and C, meant to last five years
timeline.description: Set the Area A/B/C division, a Palestinian Legislative Council, security coordination and the Joint Water Committee, pending permanent status talks due to conclude by May 1999.
timeline.problem_solved: Transferring Palestinian population centres to PA control without deciding sovereignty.
timeline.did_it_survive: Its structures still govern the West Bank three decades on; further redeployments stalled after 2000 and the IDF re-entered Area A in 2002.

timeline.name: Assassination of Yitzhak Rabin
timeline.line: An Israeli religious-nationalist opposed to Oslo kills Prime Minister Rabin
timeline.description: Rabin was shot by Yigal Amir, a Jewish extremist opposed to territorial withdrawal, after a peace rally in Tel Aviv. A wave of Hamas suicide bombings followed in early 1996, and Netanyahu narrowly won the May 1996 election.
timeline.immediate_effect: Loss of the Oslo process's principal Israeli sponsor.
timeline.long_term_effect: Showed that spoilers on both sides could reshape the process; commonly cited as a turning point, though whether Rabin would have concluded a final deal is counterfactual.

timeline.name: Western Wall tunnel clashes
timeline.line: Opening an archaeological tunnel exit near Al-Aqsa sets off gun battles between Israeli troops and PA police
timeline.description: The Netanyahu government opened an exit to the Western Wall tunnel in the Muslim Quarter; protests became firefights in which PA police and Israeli soldiers fought, with some 80 people killed. UNSCR 1073 called for reversal of acts aggravating the situation; a Washington summit calmed fighting.
timeline.immediate_effect: Emergency Washington summit.
timeline.long_term_effect: Led into the January 1997 Hebron Protocol; first time PA security forces fought the IDF.

timeline.name: Camp David summit fails
timeline.line: Clinton, Barak and Arafat fail to reach a final-status deal; each side blames the other
timeline.description: The first negotiation on all final-status issues ended without agreement, chiefly over Jerusalem and the Temple Mount and refugees. The Israeli and US official account blamed Arafat for rejecting a generous offer; Palestinian negotiators and several US participants argued the offer was neither final nor viable and that blame was shared. Talks at Taba in January 2001 narrowed gaps before Israeli elections ended them.
timeline.immediate_effect: Collapse of trust weeks before the Second Intifada.
timeline.long_term_effect: 'No partner' became a durable Israeli political belief; Palestinians cite it as proof Israel never offered sovereignty.

timeline.name: Sharon's Temple Mount visit and the outbreak of the Second Intifada
timeline.line: Opposition leader Sharon visits the Temple Mount; lethal clashes the next day grow into the Second Intifada
timeline.description: Ariel Sharon's visit with a large police escort was followed by deadly clashes at Al-Aqsa on 29 September that spread across the territories and to Arab citizens of Israel. The Mitchell Report found no persuasive evidence that the visit was more than an internal political act, nor that the PA planned the uprising, but said the visit was poorly timed; both sides dispute that reading.
timeline.immediate_effect: Sharm el-Sheikh summit (October 2000) failed to stop violence.
timeline.long_term_effect: Began five years of the conflict's deadliest violence before 2023.

timeline.name: Second (Al-Aqsa) Intifada
timeline.line: Suicide bombings and Israeli reoccupation of PA cities kill roughly 1,000 Israelis and over 3,000 Palestinians
timeline.description: Armed uprising in which Hamas, Islamic Jihad and Fatah-linked groups carried out suicide bombings inside Israel, and Israel reoccupied West Bank cities in Operation Defensive Shield (2002), besieged Arafat's compound and began the separation barrier. It faded after Arafat's death and the February 2005 Sharm el-Sheikh summit.
timeline.immediate_effect: PA security institutions destroyed; Israeli public shifted rightward on negotiations.
timeline.long_term_effect: Produced the barrier, the collapse of the Israeli peace camp, Sharon's unilateralism (Gaza disengagement) and the rise of Hamas.

timeline.name: Arab Peace Initiative
timeline.line: The Arab League offers Israel normal relations for full withdrawal and a Palestinian state
timeline.description: The Saudi-drafted initiative, endorsed at Beirut, offered normal relations with all Arab states in exchange for full withdrawal to the 1967 lines, a Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital, and a 'just' and 'agreed upon' solution to refugees under UNGA 194.
timeline.immediate_effect: Overshadowed by the Netanya bombing and Operation Defensive Shield the same week.
timeline.long_term_effect: Formally reaffirmed repeatedly; the Abraham Accords inverted its sequence (normalization before a Palestinian state), while Saudi Arabia still conditions its own normalization on a statehood path.

timeline.name: Separation barrier and the ICJ Wall opinion
timeline.line: Israel builds a barrier partly inside the West Bank; the ICJ says that route is unlawful
timeline.description: Israel began a fence-and-wall barrier in 2002 to stop suicide bombers; about 85 percent of its route runs inside the West Bank. The ICJ's 2004 advisory opinion found the portions in occupied territory contrary to international law; Israel's Supreme Court upheld the barrier in principle but ordered route changes.
timeline.immediate_effect: Sharp fall in infiltration attacks, which Israel attributes to the barrier and to IDF operations.
timeline.long_term_effect: A de facto line that shapes where Israel expects to keep settlement blocs.

timeline.name: Israel's unilateral disengagement from Gaza
timeline.line: Israel evacuates all 21 Gaza settlements and its army without an agreement
timeline.description: The Sharon government removed about 8,000 settlers from Gaza and four settlements in the northern West Bank and withdrew the army, while keeping control of Gaza's airspace, territorial waters and most crossings.
timeline.immediate_effect: PA took over Gaza; Hamas claimed the withdrawal as a victory for armed struggle.
timeline.long_term_effect: Rocket fire and the 2007 Hamas takeover made 'Gaza' the main Israeli argument against further withdrawals; whether occupation ended is disputed.

timeline.name: 2006 Lebanon War
timeline.line: A Hezbollah cross-border raid triggers a 34-day war that ends in stalemate under UNSCR 1701
timeline.description: After Hezbollah killed and captured Israeli soldiers on 12 July, Israel launched an air and later ground campaign; Hezbollah fired about 4,000 rockets into Israel. UNSCR 1701 ended fighting on 14 August, expanding UNIFIL and calling for no armed groups south of the Litani.
timeline.immediate_effect: Winograd Commission criticized Israel's decision-making; Hezbollah survived and rearmed.
timeline.long_term_effect: Seventeen years of mutual deterrence on the border; the 1701 disarmament clause went unimplemented until tested again in 2024.

timeline.name: Hamas wins elections, seizes Gaza; blockade imposed
timeline.line: Hamas wins the 2006 legislative election and in 2007 seizes Gaza; Israel and Egypt close it off
timeline.description: Hamas won the January 2006 Palestinian legislative election; the Quartet conditioned aid on recognition of Israel, renunciation of violence and acceptance of prior agreements, which Hamas refused. After a unity government collapsed, Hamas forces defeated Fatah in Gaza in June 2007. Israel declared Gaza 'hostile territory' and with Egypt imposed tight closure.
timeline.immediate_effect: Two Palestinian governments: PA in Ramallah, Hamas in Gaza; no national elections since 2006.
timeline.long_term_effect: The split undermines any single Palestinian negotiating authority and set up the cycle of Gaza wars.

timeline.name: Operation Cast Lead
timeline.line: Three-week Israeli air and ground war in Gaza after a truce lapses; ends in unilateral ceasefires
timeline.description: After a six-month Egyptian-brokered truce expired amid rocket fire, Israel struck and then invaded Gaza; about 1,400 Palestinians and 13 Israelis were killed. Both sides declared unilateral ceasefires. A UN fact-finding mission alleged war crimes by both; its head later retracted part of its findings about Israeli intent.
timeline.immediate_effect: Hamas remained in power.
timeline.long_term_effect: Template for bounded Gaza rounds.

timeline.name: Operation Pillar of Defense
timeline.line: Eight-day air campaign opens with the killing of Hamas military chief Jabari; Egypt brokers a ceasefire
timeline.description: Israel killed Ahmed Jabari and struck Gaza for eight days; rockets reached Tel Aviv and Jerusalem, many intercepted by Iron Dome. Egypt's Muslim Brotherhood government mediated a ceasefire without a ground operation.
timeline.immediate_effect: Ceasefire with vague easing of closure.
timeline.long_term_effect: Showed missile defense lets Israel fight longer rounds without ground invasion.

timeline.name: Palestine becomes a UN non-member observer State
timeline.line: UN General Assembly upgrades Palestine to non-member observer State, 138 to 9
timeline.description: Accorded Palestine non-member observer State status on the 1967 lines. Israel and the US voted against.
timeline.immediate_effect: Israel announced E1-area settlement planning; the PA gained access to treaty accession.
timeline.long_term_effect: Enabled Palestine's 2015 accession to the ICC Rome Statute, the jurisdictional basis for the 2024 arrest warrants.

timeline.name: Operation Protective Edge
timeline.line: Fifty-day Gaza war over rockets and cross-border tunnels ends with an open-ended Egyptian ceasefire
timeline.description: Followed the abduction and murder of three Israeli teenagers and a Palestinian teenager. Israel's air and ground operation targeted rockets and attack tunnels; about 2,250 Palestinians and 73 on the Israeli side were killed (UN Commission of Inquiry figures).
timeline.immediate_effect: Hamas stayed in power; reconstruction conference pledges largely unmet.
timeline.long_term_effect: Reinforced the Israeli belief that Hamas could be contained by periodic rounds.

timeline.name: Temple Mount tensions and the 2015 stabbing wave
timeline.line: Clashes at Al-Aqsa over Jewish visits feed months of lone-attacker stabbings; US-brokered understandings calm but do not end it
timeline.description: Rumours and reality of increased Jewish visits and restrictions at the compound over the Jewish holidays led to clashes and a wave of individual stabbing and ramming attacks. On 24 October Secretary Kerry announced Israeli-Jordanian understandings reaffirming that Muslims pray and non-Muslims visit, plus camera monitoring (never installed).
timeline.immediate_effect: Violence ebbed over several months.
timeline.long_term_effect: Showed leaderless violence could arise without organizational command; Jordan's custodial role was the diplomatic lever.

timeline.name: US-Israel Memorandum of Understanding on security assistance (FY2019-2028)
timeline.line: US commits $38 billion in military aid to Israel over ten years
timeline.description: Third ten-year MOU: $33 billion in Foreign Military Financing and $5 billion for missile defense, FY2019-FY2028. It is an executive understanding, not a treaty; Congress appropriates annually.
timeline.problem_solved: Predictable support for Israel's qualitative military edge after the Iran nuclear deal dispute.
timeline.did_it_survive: In force; supplemented by emergency appropriations during the 2023-25 war; negotiation of a successor MOU is pending.

timeline.name: UN Security Council Resolution 2334 on settlements
timeline.line: With a US abstention, the Security Council declares settlements have no legal validity
timeline.description: Adopted 14-0 with the Obama administration abstaining; stated settlements in territory occupied since 1967, including East Jerusalem, have no legal validity and called on states to distinguish between Israel and the occupied territories.
timeline.immediate_effect: Israeli government denounced the US; the incoming administration signalled reversal.
timeline.long_term_effect: The legal reference for the differentiation policy behind later settlement-goods restrictions.

timeline.name: Al-Aqsa metal detector crisis
timeline.line: After a shooting killed two police officers, Israel installs metal detectors at Al-Aqsa, then removes them under protest pressure
timeline.description: Arab-Israeli gunmen killed two Israeli police officers at the compound; Israel installed metal detectors, which Muslim authorities boycotted with mass street prayers. Clashes and a stabbing attack in Halamish followed; an incident at Israel's embassy in Amman gave Jordan leverage, and Israel removed the detectors and later the cameras.
timeline.immediate_effect: Worshippers returned on 27 July.
timeline.long_term_effect: A rare case of Israel reversing a security change at the site under popular pressure.

timeline.name: US recognizes Jerusalem as Israel's capital
timeline.line: The US recognizes Jerusalem as Israel's capital and moves its embassy in May 2018
timeline.description: The proclamation recognized Jerusalem as Israel's capital while stating the US took no position on the boundaries of Israeli sovereignty in the city or other final-status issues. The embassy opened on 14 May 2018 as Gaza border protests left dozens dead.
timeline.immediate_effect: The PA cut contact with the US administration; few states followed the embassy move.
timeline.long_term_effect: Removed the US from Palestinian-accepted mediation until the 2025 Gaza plan; later administrations kept the recognition.

timeline.name: Nation-State Law
timeline.line: Israel constitutionally defines itself as the nation state of the Jewish people
timeline.description: The Basic Law says the right to national self-determination in Israel is 'unique to the Jewish people' (Article 1) and that the state views 'the development of Jewish settlement as a national value' (Article 7); it downgraded Arabic from an official language to 'special status'. The Supreme Court upheld it in 2021.
timeline.immediate_effect: Protests by Druze and Arab citizens.
timeline.long_term_effect: Constitutional anchor for the settlement-as-national-value narrative.

timeline.name: Abraham Accords
timeline.line: The UAE and Bahrain normalize with Israel, which suspends West Bank annexation
timeline.description: Israel signed normalization agreements with the UAE and Bahrain in September 2020, followed by Morocco (with US recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara) and Sudan. The UAE presented Israel's suspension of annexation plans as the price.
timeline.problem_solved: Arab-Israeli normalization without first resolving the Palestinian question.
timeline.did_it_survive: Yes: no signatory severed relations during the 2023-25 Gaza war, though public engagement froze and Bahrain's parliament announced the recall of its ambassador. Saudi Arabia did not join and ties its entry to a Palestinian statehood path.

timeline.name: May 2021 Gaza war (Operation Guardian of the Walls)
timeline.line: After Al-Aqsa raids and Sheikh Jarrah evictions, Hamas fires at Jerusalem; an 11-day war follows
timeline.description: Ramadan clashes at Al-Aqsa and planned evictions in Sheikh Jarrah led Hamas to issue an ultimatum and fire rockets at Jerusalem on 10 May; 11 days of strikes and some 4,000 rockets followed, with Arab-Jewish violence in Israel's mixed cities. Egypt brokered a ceasefire.
timeline.immediate_effect: Hamas cast itself as defender of Jerusalem.
timeline.long_term_effect: Israeli policy then emphasized economic incentives (work permits) to keep Hamas quiet, part of the pre-7 October 'conception'.

timeline.name: Operation Breaking Dawn (Israel vs Islamic Jihad)
timeline.line: Three-day round against Islamic Jihad in which Hamas stays out
timeline.description: Israel pre-emptively struck PIJ commanders in Gaza; PIJ fired about 1,000 rockets. Hamas did not join, and Egypt brokered a ceasefire within three days. A similar PIJ-only round (Shield and Arrow) followed in May 2023.
timeline.immediate_effect: PIJ leadership in Gaza degraded.
timeline.long_term_effect: Read in Israel as evidence Hamas was deterred and focused on governance; after 7 October it was reinterpreted as deception.

timeline.name: Ramadan 2023 Al-Aqsa raids and rockets from Lebanon and Gaza
timeline.line: Police raids on worshippers barricaded in Al-Aqsa bring rockets from Lebanon and Gaza; limited Israeli strikes; calm within days
timeline.description: Israeli police forcibly cleared worshippers barricaded inside the Al-Aqsa mosque; about 34 rockets were fired from southern Lebanon (attributed by Israel to Hamas there) and more from Gaza. Israel struck limited targets in Lebanon and Gaza and the exchange ended within days.
timeline.immediate_effect: No wider war.
timeline.long_term_effect: Showed the Jerusalem trigger could activate a multi-front response; Hamas named its October attack 'Al-Aqsa Flood'.

timeline.name: Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, 7 October 2023
timeline.line: Hamas breaks through the Gaza fence, kills about 1,200 people in Israel and takes 251 hostages
timeline.description: Thousands of Hamas-led fighters overran border communities, army posts and a music festival, killing about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and abducting 251 hostages into Gaza. It was the deadliest day in Israel's history. IDF inquiries published in 2025 found the military had misread Hamas's intentions and capabilities.
timeline.immediate_effect: Israel declared war with the aim of destroying Hamas; Hezbollah opened fire from Lebanon on 8 October.
timeline.long_term_effect: Ended the containment policy toward Gaza, froze Saudi normalization, and triggered a regional war cycle including direct Iran-Israel exchanges.

timeline.name: Gaza war, October 2023 - October 2025
timeline.line: Two-year Israeli war in Gaza destroys much of the Strip; ends in a US-brokered ceasefire with Hamas weakened but not removed
timeline.description: Israel's air and ground campaign occupied most of Gaza and killed Hamas's senior leaders including Sinwar; the Gaza Health Ministry's toll, which the UN treats as broadly reliable and Israel disputes, exceeded 67,000 by October 2025. Truces in November 2023 and January-March 2025 released hostages before fighting resumed; the October 2025 ceasefire returned the remaining living hostages.
timeline.immediate_effect: Mass displacement of most of Gaza's population and a famine determination for Gaza City (IPC, August 2025); ICJ and ICC proceedings.
timeline.long_term_effect: Broke the bounded-rounds pattern; left Gaza's governance to an internationally endorsed transitional scheme whose implementation is unresolved.

timeline.name: ICJ provisional measures in South Africa v. Israel
timeline.line: The ICJ orders Israel to prevent genocidal acts and enable aid, without ordering a ceasefire
timeline.description: Found some of the rights claimed by South Africa plausible and ordered Israel to take all measures within its power to prevent acts under the Genocide Convention and to enable humanitarian aid; further orders followed in March and May 2024. The merits have not been decided, and the order is not a finding that genocide occurred.
timeline.immediate_effect: Diplomatic pressure on Israel's allies over arms supplies.
timeline.long_term_effect: A pending case that shapes European arms and trade decisions.

timeline.name: ICJ advisory opinion on Israel's policies in the Occupied Palestinian Territory
timeline.line: The ICJ says Israel's continued presence in the occupied territories is unlawful and should end as rapidly as possible
timeline.description: Requested by UNGA 77/247, the non-binding opinion found Israel's continued presence in the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza unlawful, settlements in breach of international law, and called on states not to recognize or aid the situation. Israel rejected it.
timeline.immediate_effect: UNGA in September 2024 demanded Israel end its presence within twelve months.
timeline.long_term_effect: Legal basis cited in the 2025 recognition wave and settlement-trade restrictions.

timeline.name: Israel-Hezbollah war, 2023-24
timeline.line: A year of cross-border fire escalates into pager attacks, Nasrallah's killing and a ground invasion, ending in a US-French ceasefire
timeline.description: Hezbollah fired on Israel from 8 October 2023 in support of Hamas, displacing northern Israeli communities. In September 2024 Israel detonated booby-trapped pagers and radios, killed Hassan Nasrallah (27 September) and invaded south Lebanon on 1 October. A ceasefire on 27 November 2024 recommitted the parties to UNSCR 1701.
timeline.immediate_effect: Hezbollah's leadership and arsenal badly degraded; Israeli troops retained positions in south Lebanon.
timeline.long_term_effect: Removed Hezbollah as an effective deterrent for Iran, contributing to the fall of Assad in December 2024; Israeli strikes in Lebanon continued under the ceasefire.

timeline.name: Knesset laws against UNRWA
timeline.line: Israel bans UNRWA operations on its sovereign territory and contact with Israeli officials
timeline.description: Two laws, in force from January 2025, barred UNRWA from operating in territory Israel considers sovereign (including East Jerusalem) and prohibited state contact with it, after Israel alleged staff participation in 7 October; a UN investigation found some staff 'may have been involved' and nine were dismissed.
timeline.immediate_effect: UNRWA's East Jerusalem operations curtailed.
timeline.long_term_effect: An attempt to dismantle the institutional carrier of refugee status (see path dependency).

timeline.name: ICC arrest warrants for Netanyahu, Gallant and Deif
timeline.line: The ICC issues arrest warrants for Israel's prime minister and former defense minister and Hamas's military chief
timeline.description: Pre-Trial Chamber I issued warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant (including starvation as a method of warfare) and for Mohammed Deif. Israel rejects the court's jurisdiction; the United States sanctioned ICC officials in 2025.
timeline.immediate_effect: Limits Netanyahu's travel to ICC member states, with some members saying they would not enforce.
timeline.long_term_effect: A standing legal constraint on the current Israeli leader.

timeline.name: January 2025 ceasefire and its collapse
timeline.line: A three-phase ceasefire frees 33 hostages, then collapses when Israel resumes strikes in March
timeline.description: The Qatari-Egyptian-US-mediated deal took effect the day before Trump's inauguration; its first phase exchanged hostages for Palestinian prisoners. Talks on the second phase (permanent ceasefire, full withdrawal) failed and Israel resumed its offensive on 18 March 2025 and halted aid entry for about 11 weeks.
timeline.immediate_effect: War resumed.
timeline.long_term_effect: Precedent that phase-one-only implementation is the likeliest failure mode of phased deals.

timeline.name: New York Declaration and Western recognition of Palestine
