timeline.line: The UN endorses a two-state roadmap 142-10; the UK, France, Canada, Australia and others recognize Palestine
timeline.description: On 12 September 2025 the General Assembly endorsed the French-Saudi New York Declaration (ceasefire, hostage release, Hamas disarmament and exclusion, a Palestinian state) by 142-10-12, with Israel and the US against. The UK, Canada, Australia and Portugal recognized Palestine on 21 September and France and others on 22 September.
timeline.immediate_effect: Israel denounced the recognitions; some Israeli ministers called for annexation in response.
timeline.long_term_effect: Made Palestine recognized by most of the G7's European members, without changing control on the ground.

timeline.name: October 2025 Gaza ceasefire under the 20-point plan
timeline.line: Hamas returns the living hostages and Israel pulls back to a 'yellow line' under Trump's 20-point plan; disarmament and governance are left for later
timeline.description: After the 29 September 2025 White House plan, Israel and Hamas agreed its first phase: the ceasefire took effect on 10 October, the 20 living hostages were released on 13 October in exchange for Palestinian prisoners, and the IDF withdrew to an interim line while retaining much of the Strip. Hamas disarmament, an International Stabilization Force, a technocratic Palestinian committee and further Israeli withdrawal were deferred to later phases.
timeline.immediate_effect: End of major combat; aid access increased; recurrent lethal violations by both sides.
timeline.long_term_effect: As of mid-2026 the second phase remained largely unimplemented, reproducing the Oslo pattern of an interim arrangement with the hard issues deferred.

timeline.name: UN Security Council Resolution 2803 (Board of Peace and Stabilization Force)
timeline.line: The Security Council endorses the Gaza plan, a Board of Peace and an International Stabilization Force
timeline.description: Adopted 13-0 with China and Russia abstaining; welcomed the Comprehensive Plan, the Board of Peace as a transitional administration for Gaza and authorized an International Stabilization Force, with PA control conditioned on reforms and a possible pathway to Palestinian self-determination.
timeline.immediate_effect: International legal mandate for the post-war scheme; Hamas rejected disarmament provisions.
timeline.long_term_effect: The operative framework for Gaza's governance; its implementation is the main open question of the file.

territories.name: West Bank

historical_control.note: military then mandate administration
annexed April 1950; the annexation was recognized by very few states
military occupation; since Oslo II the PA has civil control in Areas A and B

current_claims.basis: 1988 declaration on the 1967 lines; UNGA 67/19; recognition by most UN members

Israel has not annexed the West Bank but asserts historical and legal rights, calls it disputed rather than occupied, and its 2022 government guidelines claim a Jewish right to all of the Land of Israel

territories.recognition: Jordan relinquished its claim in 1988. UNSCR 2334 (2016) and the ICJ (2004, 2024) treat it as occupied territory and settlements as unlawful; the 2024 advisory opinion called Israel's continued presence unlawful. Israel rejects these findings. The United States has shifted position on settlement legality across administrations.
territories.de_facto_note: Oslo II Areas: A (PA civil and security control), B (PA civil, Israeli security), C (about 60 percent of the territory, full Israeli control). East Jerusalem is treated separately.
significance: core of any Palestinian state
national-religious (Hebron, Shechem/Nablus, biblical heartland)
strategic geography (highlands overlooking Israel's coastal plain)
shared Mountain Aquifer

territories.name: Gaza Strip

historical_control.note: administered, never annexed
military occupation; PA self-rule in parts from 1994
under Israeli-Egyptian closure from 2007; Israeli ground forces held large parts of the Strip from late 2023

current_claims.basis: part of the 1967 territories; UNGA 67/19

territories.recognition: Israel claims no sovereignty. Whether Israel remained an occupying power after the 2005 withdrawal is contested: Israel says no; the ICJ in 2024 said its obligations continue in proportion to its effective control. UNSCR 2803 (2025) endorsed a transitional Board of Peace and an International Stabilization Force pending PA reform.
territories.de_facto_note: Under the October 2025 ceasefire the IDF withdrew to a 'yellow line' and still held a large share of the Strip, while Hamas remained the armed authority in the rest. As of mid-2026 advocacy and press assessments reported little progress on the plan's second phase (disarmament, ISF deployment, further withdrawal). Verify against current reporting before use.
significance: humanitarian (about two million people in 365 square km)
the base of Hamas's armed wing
Egypt's Rafah border and the Philadelphi corridor

territories.name: East Jerusalem and the Old City

historical_control.note: Israeli law applied June 1967; Basic Law: Jerusalem 1980

current_claims.basis: Basic Law: Jerusalem (1980), 'complete and united' capital
capital of the declared State of Palestine

territories.recognition: UNSCR 478 (1980) declared the Jerusalem Law null and void; most states keep embassies in Tel Aviv. The US recognized Jerusalem as Israel's capital in December 2017 while stating it took no position on the boundaries of Israeli sovereignty in the city. UNGA 181 had proposed an international regime for Jerusalem. Jordan's special role at the Muslim holy shrines is recognized in Article 9 of the 1994 treaty.
territories.de_facto_note: The Jordanian-funded Islamic Waqf administers the Haram al-Sharif/Temple Mount under Israeli security control; the post-1967 'status quo' bars non-Muslim prayer there, a rule under growing pressure.
significance: religious (Judaism, Islam, Christianity)
the most reliable escalation trigger in the conflict
final-status issue under Oslo I Article V

territories.name: Golan Heights

historical_control.note: French mandate before 1946

current_claims.basis: pre-1967 sovereignty; UNSCR 242 and 497
Golan Heights Law (1981)

territories.recognition: UNSCR 497 (1981) declared the Israeli law null and void. The United States recognized Israeli sovereignty in March 2019; almost no other state has. After the fall of Assad in December 2024 Israeli forces entered the 1974 disengagement buffer zone.
significance: military (high ground over the Galilee)
water (Jordan River headwaters, Sea of Galilee catchment)

territories.name: Sinai Peninsula

historical_control.note: Israel also held it briefly in 1956-57

current_claims.basis: sovereignty confirmed by the 1979 treaty; Taba returned after 1988 arbitration

territories.recognition: Egyptian sovereignty is universally recognized; the treaty's military annex limits Egyptian forces in zones of Sinai, with the Multinational Force and Observers verifying.
significance: the precedent for full withdrawal in exchange for a peace treaty
Rafah crossing and Philadelphi corridor border Gaza

lessons.name: Israel trades territory for peace with states, not with non-state actors
lessons.description: Israel returned all of Sinai for a treaty with Egypt and settled borders with Jordan, both states able to enforce commitments; it has not concluded a final agreement with the PLO or withdrawn by agreement from Palestinian territory. The literature reads this as a preference for counterparts with state enforcement capacity; the alternative reading is that the West Bank and Jerusalem carry national-religious weight Sinai never did.

lessons.name: Israel: periodic force to degrade, not defeat, entrenched non-state enemies ('mowing the grass')
lessons.description: Inbar and Shamir (2014) described Israeli strategy toward Hamas and Hezbollah as attrition to degrade capabilities and restore deterrence, accepting that the enemy cannot be eliminated at acceptable cost. It was an academic characterization rather than published doctrine. The 2023-25 war's declared aim of destroying Hamas repudiated it.

lessons.name: Israel: a fixed intelligence 'conception' of enemy intent failed in 1973 and 2023
lessons.description: The Agranat Commission found that Israeli intelligence in 1973 was captive to a concept that Egypt would not attack; IDF inquiries published in 2025 found the army believed Hamas was deterred and focused on governance. The parallel is drawn by Israeli commissions and commentators; whether reforms prevent recurrence is not established.

lessons.name: Hamas: from rejecting any settlement (1988) to accepting a 1967-lines state without recognizing Israel (2017)
lessons.description: The 1988 Covenant called for Islamic rule over all Palestine and rejected negotiations; the 2017 Document of General Principles accepted a Palestinian state on the 1967 lines as a 'formula of national consensus' while refusing to recognize Israel or renounce armed struggle. Both are written texts; whether 2017 was tactical is interpretation, and 7 October is the principal evidence cited for that reading.

lessons.name: Israel: unilateral withdrawals (Lebanon 2000, Gaza 2005) are read as producing hostile bases
lessons.description: Mainstream Israeli political discourse treats the 2000 Lebanon and 2005 Gaza withdrawals as having emboldened Hezbollah and Hamas, and this is the main public argument against West Bank withdrawal. Critics argue the lesson is about unilateralism and the 2007 siege rather than withdrawal itself. The interpretation is widespread; its causal claim is disputed.

lessons.name: PA: threats to end security coordination are rarely carried through because the PA depends on it
lessons.description: Inference from repeated announcements and the single sustained suspension (May-November 2020), which ended when the PA needed Israeli-collected tax revenue. A PA facing collapse or a successor to Abbas could act differently.

tendencies.name: Israel fights non-state enemies in bounded rounds ended by third-party-mediated ceasefires
current_evidence: The 2023-25 Gaza war still ended through Egyptian, Qatari and US mediation, but only after two years and with the stated aim of removing Hamas; since the November 2024 Lebanon ceasefire and the October 2025 Gaza ceasefire Israel has continued strikes it describes as enforcement.
tendencies.caveat: The pattern held 2008-2022 under a leadership that judged Hamas deterred; 7 October changed Israel's risk tolerance, and post-2023 behaviour (holding territory, strikes during ceasefires) looks different. Do not project the pre-2023 duration base rate onto post-2023 rounds.

tendencies.name: Changes at Jerusalem's holy sites are the most reliable trigger for multi-front escalation
current_evidence: Hamas named its October 2023 attack 'Al-Aqsa Flood'; Israeli ministers' visits and the growth of Jewish prayer at the compound since 2023 are cited by Jordan and the PA as violations of the status quo.
tendencies.caveat: Contradicting cases show de-escalation when Israel reversed the change (2017) or when Jordan brokered understandings (2015); 7 October was planned for years, so the holy-site framing was partly justification rather than trigger. Selection bias: flashpoints that fizzled are underrecorded.

tendencies.name: Arab states normalize with Israel when their own interests require it, ahead of a Palestinian settlement
contradicting: Saudi Arabia froze normalization talks after 7 October 2023 and publicly conditions them on an irreversible path to a Palestinian state.
current_evidence: No Abraham Accords state or treaty partner cut diplomatic relations during the 2023-25 war; Saudi Arabia co-sponsored the 2025 New York Declaration rather than normalizing.
tendencies.caveat: Normalization has come from states with a specific payoff (Sinai, US security guarantees, Western Sahara recognition, sanctions removal); public opinion constraints rose sharply after 2023. The largest prize, Saudi Arabia, is the case that currently contradicts the pattern.

tendencies.name: Israeli settlement in the West Bank and East Jerusalem has grown under governments of left and right
contradicting: The 2009-10 ten-month West Bank construction moratorium under US pressure; the 2020 suspension of annexation for the Abraham Accords.
current_evidence: The 2022 government guidelines claim a right to all the Land of Israel; settlement planning approvals in 2023-25, including the E1 plan east of Jerusalem, were at record levels by Peace Now's count.
tendencies.caveat: Evacuations did happen when the government judged the strategic payoff large (Sinai for peace, Gaza for security); the tendency describes the default, not a law. Population data come from Israel's statistics bureau, planning data largely from an advocacy NGO.

path_dependencies.name: From Oslo's deferred issues to two Palestinian authorities and a permanent interim

chain.step: 1993 Oslo I defers Jerusalem, refugees, settlements, borders and security to later talks
1995 Oslo II creates Areas A/B/C as a five-year interim
2000 Camp David fails; the Second Intifada destroys trust and PA institutions
2005 unilateral Gaza withdrawal without an agreed successor
2006-07 Hamas election win and Gaza takeover split Palestinian governance
2025 Gaza ceasefire again defers disarmament and governance to later phases
Current constraint: Area C under Israeli control, no single Palestinian authority able to deliver security, and every framework interim by design

path_dependencies.description: Each arrow is a hypothesis about causation. The documents and dates are established; how much the interim design, as opposed to violence, settlement growth or leadership choices, caused the stalemate is disputed.

path_dependencies.name: From the 1948 displacement to an unresolved refugee question

chain.step: 1947-49 displacement of some 700,000-750,000 Palestinian Arabs
UNGA 194 paragraph 11 on return or compensation
UNRWA registers refugees and descendants, institutionalizing status across generations
Oslo I defers refugees to permanent status
2024 Knesset laws move to shut UNRWA out
Current constraint: millions of registered refugees; return is a Palestinian core demand and an Israeli red line

path_dependencies.description: The documents are primary; the claim that UNRWA's registration rules perpetuate the conflict is an Israeli interpretation, and the claim that dismantling UNRWA would end refugee status is contested by Palestinians and the UN.

narratives.name: Palestinians: the Nakba as an ongoing dispossession
narratives.historical_event: 1947-49 displacement and depopulation of villages
narratives.modern_interpretation: Palestinian leaders frame 1948 as the start of a continuing Nakba extended by occupation, settlement and the Gaza war, which grounds the right of return and the rejection of recognizing Israel as a Jewish state. The displacement is documented; 'ongoing Nakba' is a political reading, contested by Israelis who frame 1948 as a defensive war the Arab side started.
used_in: the UN's first official Nakba commemoration in May 2023
PA and Hamas statements during the Gaza war

narratives.name: Israel: a refuge that must defend itself by itself after the Holocaust and 7 October
narratives.historical_event: The Holocaust; the 1948 invasion; the 1973 surprise; 7 October 2023
narratives.modern_interpretation: Israeli leaders describe 7 October as the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust and justify maximal war aims and independence of action from allies and international courts in those terms. The events are documented; the inference that international constraints are illegitimate is a political reading.
used_in: the Yom HaShoah, Memorial Day and Independence Day sequence
Israel's rejection of ICJ and ICC proceedings

narratives.name: Israeli right: an exclusive Jewish right to Judea and Samaria
narratives.historical_event: Biblical and ancient Jewish presence; the 1967 capture of the West Bank
narratives.modern_interpretation: The 2018 Nation-State Law calls Jewish settlement a national value and the 2022 government guidelines assert an 'exclusive and unquestionable' right to all areas of the Land of Israel, used to oppose Palestinian statehood and support annexation. The ancient history is documented; its translation into present sovereignty is a political claim rejected by the ICJ and most states.

narratives.name: Palestinian and Islamist: 'Al-Aqsa is in danger'
narratives.historical_event: 1929 Western Wall dispute; 1967 capture of the Old City; 2000 Sharon visit
narratives.modern_interpretation: Hamas, the PA, Jordan and Islamist movements cast Israeli security measures and Jewish visits as a plan to change the compound's status or divide it, which mobilizes across factions and borders. Growing Jewish prayer at the site and ministerial visits are documented; a coordinated plan to destroy the mosque is not.
used_in: Hamas's name for the 7 October attack ('Al-Aqsa Flood')

2006 Lebanon War
Operation Cast Lead

Operation Protective Edge

Operation Breaking Dawn (Israel vs Islamic Jihad)

asymmetric_rocket_conflict_round.selection_note: Cases are named Israeli military operations or wars against a non-state armed group that fires rockets or missiles from adjacent territory (Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad in Gaza, Hezbollah in Lebanon), 2006-2024. The set is the named rounds only: it omits the hundreds of smaller exchanges that ended within a day and the 2000-2005 intifada (a different form of conflict). 'limited_conflict' means a bounded round ended by a mediated or unilateral ceasefire with the group still governing or armed; 'war' means ground invasion aimed at removing or crippling the group. Famous rounds are over-represented relative to quiet periods, so the set says how rounds END, not how often they START. The 2023-25 Gaza war and the 2024 Lebanon war broke the earlier 'bounded round' pattern; weight post-October 2023 cases accordingly.

cases.name: Egyptian mobilization into Sinai, May 1967
Egyptian and Syrian mobilization under exercise cover, October 1973
Exercise Brasstacks crisis
1990 Kashmir crisis
Iraqi buildup on the Kuwaiti border, July 1990
India's Operation Parakram
Russia-Georgia war
Seizure of Crimea and outbreak of the Donbas war
Doklam standoff
Russian spring 2021 buildup on Ukraine's border
Winter 2021-22 buildup and full-scale invasion

pooled.note: n=11; pooling moves it 42% toward the parent distribution over 101 classed cases.

border_mobilization.selection_note: Cases are large, visible troop concentrations on a neighbour's border. The set is drawn from well-documented crises and is biased toward mobilizations that became famous because they led to war; quiet buildups that dissolved are under-recorded. Treat the war share as an upper bound on the prior, not a point estimate.

Sharon's Temple Mount visit and the outbreak of the Second Intifada
Temple Mount tensions and the 2015 stabbing wave
Al-Aqsa metal detector crisis
Ramadan 2023 Al-Aqsa raids and rockets from Lebanon and Gaza

pooled.note: n=5 is below the low-n floor of 8: the pooled figure is 62% the parent class, not this class. Publish the interval, name n, and say the reference class is thin.

jerusalem_holy_site_flashpoint.selection_note: Cases are crises whose proximate trigger was a change, or a perceived change, at the Haram al-Sharif/Temple Mount or its surroundings (tunnel opening, a political visit, security installations, police raids). Assembled from episodes that produced multi-day violence and international diplomacy; flashpoints that faded within a day are omitted, so the set is biased toward escalation. The May 2021 Sheikh Jarrah/Al-Aqsa crisis is filed under asymmetric_rocket_conflict_round because it became a Gaza war round; count it here too when asking how holy-site triggers end.
jerusalem_holy_site_flashpoint.note: only 5 comparable cases: use as a rough prior, not a percentage

timeline.name: Japan annexes Korea
timeline.line: Japan annexes Korea; 35 years of colonial rule
timeline.description: The annexation treaty ended Korean sovereignty until 1945.
timeline.immediate_effect: Colonial administration and industrialization concentrated in the north.
timeline.long_term_effect: Colonial-era grievances (forced labour, 'comfort women') still drive ROK-Japan relations and complicate trilateral security cooperation.

timeline.name: Korea divided at the 38th parallel
timeline.line: US and Soviet occupation zones split the peninsula; two states follow in 1948
timeline.description: A line chosen hastily in Washington for accepting the Japanese surrender became the boundary between rival states proclaimed in August and September 1948.
timeline.immediate_effect: Two governments each claiming the whole peninsula.
timeline.long_term_effect: The division is the root of every subsequent crisis.

timeline.name: Korean War
timeline.line: North Korea invades; UN forces and then China intervene; armistice restores roughly the original line
timeline.description: The North's June 1950 invasion nearly took the whole peninsula; the UN counteroffensive reached the Yalu; Chinese intervention pushed the front back to near the 38th parallel where it stalemated.
timeline.immediate_effect: Millions dead; the peninsula devastated.
timeline.long_term_effect: Permanent US troop presence in the South, the PRC-DPRK bond, and the North's siege identity.

timeline.name: Korean Armistice Agreement
timeline.line: Armistice halts the fighting; no peace treaty has ever followed
timeline.description: Signed by the UNC, the KPA and the Chinese People's Volunteers; the ROK did not sign. Established the DMZ and the Military Armistice Commission.
timeline.problem_solved: Stopping the fighting.
timeline.did_it_survive: In force for seven decades, with repeated DPRK declarations that it no longer recognizes it; no peace treaty.

timeline.name: US-ROK Mutual Defense Treaty
timeline.line: US-ROK alliance treaty; US forces stationed in Korea ever since
timeline.description: Each party would act to meet a common danger in accordance with constitutional processes; the basis for US Forces Korea, about 28,500 personnel.
timeline.problem_solved: Reassuring Seoul against a renewed invasion and restraining it from unilateral action.
timeline.did_it_survive: Yes, through repeated crises and burden-sharing disputes.

timeline.name: PRC-DPRK Treaty of Friendship, Co-operation and Mutual Assistance
timeline.line: China's only formal mutual-assistance treaty, still in force
timeline.description: Article 2 commits each side to immediate military and other assistance if the other is attacked.
timeline.problem_solved: Soviet-Chinese competition for Pyongyang.
timeline.did_it_survive: Renewed in 1981 and 2001; Beijing's reading of the automaticity of Article 2 is deliberately ambiguous.

timeline.name: Blue House raid and USS Pueblo seizure
timeline.description: A commando team attempted to assassinate President Park; two days later the DPRK seized USS Pueblo. Dozens killed in the raid and its pursuit; the Pueblo crew was released after eleven months of negotiation.

timeline.name: Panmunjom axe murder incident
timeline.description: Two US officers killed in the Joint Security Area; the US responded with a massive show of force to cut the tree (Operation Paul Bunyan) and Kim Il Sung expressed regret.

timeline.name: Rangoon bombing
timeline.description: DPRK agents bombed a ceremony in Rangoon, killing 21 including four ROK cabinet ministers; Burma severed relations; no ROK military retaliation.

timeline.name: US-DPRK Agreed Framework
timeline.line: Agreed Framework freezes the plutonium program in exchange for reactors and fuel; collapses in 2002
timeline.description: The DPRK froze its Yongbyon reactors in return for light-water reactors and heavy fuel oil.
timeline.problem_solved: The 1994 crisis in which the US considered strikes on Yongbyon.
timeline.did_it_survive: Collapsed in 2002 over a suspected uranium program; the DPRK withdrew from the NPT in 2003 and tested in 2006.

timeline.name: First North Korean nuclear test
timeline.line: First nuclear test; UN sanctions begin
timeline.description: UNSCR 1718 followed within days; five more tests followed through 2017.
timeline.immediate_effect: Sanctions regime established.
timeline.long_term_effect: Denuclearization became the frame for all subsequent diplomacy, and then an unrealistic one.

timeline.name: Sinking of ROKS Cheonan
timeline.line: ROKS Cheonan sunk by a North Korean torpedo, 46 sailors killed; Seoul responds with sanctions, not force
timeline.description: The multinational investigation attributed the sinking to a DPRK torpedo; Pyongyang denies it. The ROK imposed the May 24 measures suspending most inter-Korean trade.

timeline.name: Shelling of Yeonpyeong Island
timeline.line: North Korean artillery shells Yeonpyeong; the ROK returns fire; four killed
timeline.description: The first artillery attack on ROK territory since 1953, during an ROK live-fire drill. The ROK fired back and later changed rules of engagement to allow disproportionate response.

timeline.name: DMZ landmine maiming and artillery exchange
timeline.description: Two ROK soldiers maimed by mines; the ROK resumed loudspeaker broadcasts; an artillery exchange followed on 20 August; a 25 August agreement ended the standoff with a DPRK expression of regret.

timeline.name: 2017 thermonuclear test and ICBM launches
timeline.line: Sixth nuclear test and first ICBMs able to reach the US mainland; 'fire and fury' rhetoric; then a pivot to summits
timeline.description: The September 2017 test was assessed as thermonuclear; the Hwasong-15 launch in November demonstrated intercontinental range. UNSCR 2397 followed.
timeline.immediate_effect: Peak sanctions and war talk.
timeline.long_term_effect: Kim declared the nuclear force 'complete' and moved to diplomacy from a position of demonstrated capability.

timeline.name: Singapore and Hanoi summits
timeline.line: First US-DPRK leaders' summit; Hanoi collapses over sanctions relief for Yongbyon
timeline.description: The Singapore statement committed to 'work toward complete denuclearization' without a definition; Hanoi ended without agreement when the US rejected Yongbyon-for-major-sanctions-relief.
timeline.immediate_effect: Test moratorium 2018-2021.
timeline.long_term_effect: Kim concluded that diplomacy on those terms would not deliver; the 2022 law followed.

timeline.name: DPRK law declaring nuclear status irreversible
timeline.line: Law states the nuclear status is irreversible and authorizes preemptive use if the leadership is threatened
timeline.description: Codified conditions for nuclear use, including a decapitation attempt, and ruled out denuclearization as a negotiating subject.
timeline.immediate_effect: Denuclearization talks foreclosed by DPRK law.
timeline.long_term_effect: The documented doctrine against which any future DPRK offer should be read.

timeline.name: Kim abandons unification; ROK designated the principal enemy
timeline.line: Kim declares the two Koreas separate hostile states and orders unification institutions dismantled
timeline.description: A break with the unification framework maintained since 1948; inter-Korean agencies were abolished and the constitution ordered amended.
timeline.immediate_effect: Inter-Korean channels closed.
timeline.long_term_effect: Removes the 'one nation' restraint on the use of force against the South, in Pyongyang's own framing. Whether behaviour follows the framing is an open question.

timeline.name: DPRK-Russia Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty
timeline.line: Putin and Kim sign a mutual-assistance treaty; North Korean troops fight in Kursk within months
timeline.description: Article 4 provides for military and other assistance if either is attacked. The ROK NIS and the US assessed in October 2024 that thousands of DPRK troops had deployed to Russia; Pyongyang acknowledged the deployment in April 2025.
timeline.problem_solved: Russia's munitions and manpower shortfall; DPRK's isolation and technology needs.
timeline.did_it_survive: In force and operationalized within four months, which is faster than most alliances are tested.

territories.name: Northern Limit Line and the West Sea islands

historical_control.note: line drawn unilaterally by the UNC after the armistice; the five islands are ROK-administered

current_claims.basis: de facto boundary since 1953
rejects the NLL; proposed its own line in 1999 and 2007

territories.recognition: The armistice does not define a maritime boundary; the NLL has no treaty basis but has functioned as the line for seven decades.
significance: military (site of the 1999, 2002, 2009 naval clashes and the 2010 Yeonpyeong shelling)
economic (crab fishing grounds)

lessons.name: ROK: security rests on the US alliance and combined deterrence
lessons.description: Stated in every ROK defense white paper; institutionalized in the Combined Forces Command and extended-deterrence consultations (Washington Declaration, 2023).

lessons.name: DPRK: nuclear weapons guarantee regime survival and are not negotiable
lessons.description: Written into the 2022 nuclear forces law and the 2023 constitutional amendment. The regime cites Iraq and Libya as what happens to states that disarm; that inference is the regime's own stated reasoning.

lessons.name: China: prevent a US-aligned unified Korea on the Yalu
lessons.description: The standard reading of China's 1950 intervention and continued support for Pyongyang despite nuclear tests. Chinese documents describe 'peace and stability' priorities; the buffer logic is inferred by analysts and by Chinese scholars, not stated as doctrine.

tendencies.name: North Korea alternates lethal or nuclear provocation with offers to talk, keeping each below the threshold of war
contradicting: Since 2019 the DPRK has refused talks entirely and in 2024 renounced unification, so the bargaining half of the cycle has not recurred under Kim Jong Un's later period; the 1950 invasion itself is the case where provocation was war.
current_evidence: Russia now supplies what bargaining with Washington used to: the incentive to return to the cycle is weaker than at any point since 1991.
tendencies.caveat: The cycle was a product of isolation. With Russian backing the regime may not need it, so the historical pattern may be less predictive now than at any time since it was identified.

path_dependencies.name: From an armistice without a peace treaty to a nuclear-armed 'two hostile states'

chain.step: 1953 armistice leaves a legal state of war and a UNC presence
US-ROK treaty stations US forces permanently
Pyongyang frames the US presence as a 'hostile policy' justifying a deterrent
Nuclear status written into law (2022) and constitution (2023)
Current constraint: denuclearization is legally foreclosed by the DPRK and politically required by the US and ROK; there is no overlap to negotiate in

path_dependencies.description: Documents at each step; the causal arrows are assessments.

narratives.name: DPRK: a besieged fortress facing a US hostile policy since 1950
narratives.historical_event: 1950-53 war and US bombing; sanctions since 2006
narratives.modern_interpretation: State media frames every sanction and exercise as continuation of the war. The bombing campaign is documented; the claim of unbroken US intent to destroy the state is regime narrative.

narratives.name: ROK: peaceful unification as constitutional duty
narratives.historical_event: 1945 division
narratives.modern_interpretation: Article 4 of the ROK constitution mandates pursuit of peaceful unification; policy oscillates between engagement and pressure by administration. The 2024 DPRK renunciation left the ROK narrative without a counterpart.

Panmunjom axe murder incident
Rangoon bombing
Sinking of ROKS Cheonan
Shelling of Yeonpyeong Island
DMZ landmine maiming and artillery exchange

pooled.note: n=6 is below the low-n floor of 8: the pooled figure is 57% the parent class, not this class. Publish the interval, name n, and say the reference class is thin.

dprk_lethal_provocation.selection_note: Cases are North Korean actions that killed South Korean or US personnel or civilians. Outcome 'limited_conflict' means a bounded exchange of fire; 'de_escalation' means no military retaliation. No case escalated to war. The set is not exhaustive of every DMZ incident, only of the well-documented lethal ones, so it is a floor on frequency and a fair sample of outcomes.
dprk_lethal_provocation.note: only 6 comparable cases: use as a rough prior, not a percentage

why_it_matters.name: Israel withdraws from south Lebanon
why_it_matters.line: Israel leaves its south Lebanon security zone; Hezbollah claims the victory and keeps its arms over Shebaa

why_it_matters.name: The Houthi slogan and the Saada wars
why_it_matters.line: A Zaydi revival movement adopts 'Death to America, Death to Israel' and survives six wars with the Yemeni state

why_it_matters.name: UN Security Council Resolution 1701
why_it_matters.line: Resolution 1701 ends the 2006 war and bars armed men other than the army and UNIFIL south of the Litani

why_it_matters.name: Hezbollah fights openly for Assad at Qusayr
why_it_matters.line: Nasrallah declares Syria 'our battle'; Hezbollah and the Syrian army retake Qusayr

why_it_matters.name: Sistani's call to arms and the rise of the PMF
why_it_matters.line: After Mosul falls, Sistani's call to arms creates the Popular Mobilization Forces

why_it_matters.name: Houthis take Sanaa
why_it_matters.line: The Houthis seize the capital; Hadi resigns in January 2015

why_it_matters.name: Pager attacks and the killing of Nasrallah
why_it_matters.line: Exploding pagers maim Hezbollah's ranks; ten days later Israel kills Nasrallah

why_it_matters.name: Lebanese cabinet orders a state monopoly of arms
why_it_matters.line: Lebanon's cabinet tasks the army with disarming Hezbollah; Hezbollah says it will ignore the decision

why_it_matters.name: Lebanon bans Hezbollah's military activity as Hezbollah joins the Iran war
why_it_matters.line: Hezbollah fires on Israel for Iran; the same day Lebanon's government bans its military activity

timeline.name: SCIRI and its Badr armed wing founded in Iran
timeline.line: Iraqi Shia exiles found SCIRI in Iran; the IRGC raises its Badr wing
timeline.description: During the Iran-Iraq War, Iraqi Shia exiles formed SCIRI in Iran under Mohammad Baqir al-Hakim, and the IRGC organised its armed wing, Badr, in 1982-83. The exact founding month is not established in the sources used.
timeline.immediate_effect: An Iraqi armed force fighting on Iran's side against Saddam.
timeline.long_term_effect: Badr returned in 2003 and became a core of Iraq's security institutions and the PMF, the oldest thread in Iran's Iraqi network.

timeline.name: Taif Agreement (Document of National Accord)
timeline.line: Taif ends Lebanon's civil war and orders militias disbanded, but Hezbollah keeps its arms as 'resistance'
timeline.description: The agreement required all militias to hand weapons to the state within six months and called for all steps needed to liberate Lebanese land from Israeli occupation. Hezbollah read the second clause as exempting its 'resistance'; the text itself names no exemption.
timeline.problem_solved: Ending the 1975-90 civil war.
timeline.did_it_survive: Yes as Lebanon's constitutional base (1990 amendments); the disarmament clause was never applied to Hezbollah.

timeline.name: IRGC Quds Force formalised as the external-operations arm
timeline.line: Iran formalises the Quds Force to run its partners abroad
timeline.description: The Quds Force took shape as a distinct IRGC command for extraterritorial operations. RFE/RL dates this to the late 1980s; other accounts say about 1990.
timeline.immediate_effect: A single command for the Lebanese, Iraqi and Afghan partner networks.
timeline.long_term_effect: The institution that built the axis. The US designated it under E.O. 13224 in 2007.

timeline.name: Israel kills Hezbollah leader Abbas al-Musawi
timeline.line: Musawi is killed; Nasrallah succeeds him; the Buenos Aires embassy is bombed a month later
timeline.description: Israeli helicopters killed Musawi and his family. Hezbollah fired rockets into northern Israel, and the 17 March embassy bombing in Buenos Aires was later attributed by Argentine courts to Iran and Hezbollah (denied by both).
timeline.immediate_effect: Nasrallah took over.
timeline.long_term_effect: Coded as the axis's response, not Iran's alone: the retaliation was delayed, far away and deniable. Attribution is contested.

timeline.name: Bombing of the Israeli embassy in Buenos Aires
timeline.line: A car bomb kills 29 at Israel's embassy in Buenos Aires, a month after Israel killed Hezbollah's leader
timeline.description: A car bomb destroyed the embassy and killed 29. In 2024 Argentina's Federal Court of Cassation ruled that Iran ordered it and Hezbollah carried it out. Hezbollah officially denied the attack and Iran denies involvement.
timeline.immediate_effect: The first attack on Israeli targets outside the Middle East that was attributed to the axis.
timeline.long_term_effect: The precedent for reading axis retaliation as possible far from the front, on a delay.

timeline.name: AMIA Jewish community centre bombing, Buenos Aires
timeline.line: The AMIA bombing kills 85; Argentine courts later attribute it to Iran and Hezbollah
timeline.description: A truck bomb killed 85 at the AMIA building. On 11 April 2024 the Cassation court classed it as a crime against humanity ordered by Iran and carried out by Hezbollah, linking the motive to Argentina's cancelled nuclear contracts. Iran calls the ruling baseless and politically motivated.
timeline.immediate_effect: A decades-long investigation and Interpol notices.
timeline.long_term_effect: A live legal and diplomatic dispute between Argentina and Iran.

timeline.name: Operation Grapes of Wrath
timeline.line: Israel's 1996 campaign against Hezbollah ends in a written understanding after the Qana shelling
timeline.description: Israeli shelling of the UNIFIL compound at Qana on 18 April killed 106 civilians sheltering there; a UN investigator found gross error 'unlikely', while Israel called it an accident. The April Understanding ended the round.
timeline.immediate_effect: Rules limiting fire on civilians.
timeline.long_term_effect: International pressure after mass civilian deaths ended the operation early.

timeline.name: April Understanding (Israel-Lebanon)
timeline.line: A written 'rules of the game' bars fire on civilians by both sides
timeline.description: It ended Operation Grapes of Wrath: armed groups in Lebanon would not fire into Israel and Israel would not fire at civilian targets in Lebanon. A US-France-Syria-Lebanon-Israel monitoring group oversaw it.
timeline.problem_solved: Limiting the fighting to military targets in the security zone.
timeline.did_it_survive: Until the 2000 withdrawal made it moot.

timeline.name: US designates Hezbollah a Foreign Terrorist Organization
timeline.line: Hezbollah is among the first FTO designations
timeline.description: The State Department listed Hezbollah under INA section 219 in the first round of FTO designations.
timeline.immediate_effect: Material support to Hezbollah became a US crime.
timeline.long_term_effect: The legal base for later designations of its financiers and media.

timeline.name: Israel withdraws from south Lebanon
timeline.line: Israel leaves its south Lebanon security zone; Hezbollah claims the victory and keeps its arms over Shebaa
timeline.description: Israel completed a unilateral withdrawal. The UN certified it as meeting resolution 425 along a 'Blue Line' that left the Shebaa Farms on the Golan side. Lebanon and Hezbollah say the farms are Lebanese.
timeline.immediate_effect: Hezbollah's prestige peaked; Nasrallah called Israel 'weaker than a spider's web'.
timeline.long_term_effect: The Shebaa claim gave Hezbollah a continuing rationale for arms; the 'resistance works' story underpins the axis's self-image.

timeline.name: The Houthi slogan and the Saada wars
timeline.line: A Zaydi revival movement adopts 'Death to America, Death to Israel' and survives six wars with the Yemeni state
timeline.description: Hussein al-Houthi's Believing Youth first chanted the sarkha in January 2002. Six rounds of fighting with the Saleh government (June 2004 - February 2010) killed Hussein in 2004 and brought his brother Abdul-Malik to the leadership.
timeline.immediate_effect: A hardened armed movement in Saada.
timeline.long_term_effect: Its identity and cohesion predate any significant Iranian role; this is the basis of the 'not a proxy' reading.

timeline.name: UN Security Council Resolution 1559
timeline.line: The UN calls for foreign forces to leave Lebanon and all militias to disarm
timeline.description: Paragraph 2 called on remaining foreign forces to withdraw; paragraph 3 called for 'the disbanding and disarmament of all Lebanese and non-Lebanese militias'.
timeline.immediate_effect: International backing for ending Syria's presence.
timeline.long_term_effect: The first UN disarmament text aimed in practice at Hezbollah, restated in 1701 and in every later arrangement.

timeline.name: Assassination of Rafik Hariri and Syrian withdrawal
timeline.line: Hariri is killed; mass protests end Syria's 29-year military presence
timeline.description: A truck bomb killed former PM Hariri. Syria completed its withdrawal on 26 April 2005 (UN-verified in May). The Special Tribunal convicted Hezbollah member Salim Ayyash in 2020 and two more on appeal in 2022, but found no proof that Hezbollah's leadership or Syria was involved; Hezbollah rejected the tribunal.
timeline.immediate_effect: End of Syrian tutelage; Lebanon split into March 8 and March 14 camps.
timeline.long_term_effect: Hezbollah became the main guarantor of the axis inside Lebanese politics.

timeline.name: Iran-Syria defence agreement
timeline.line: Iran and Syria sign a defence pact 'against common threats'
timeline.description: Defence ministers Najjar and Turkmani signed it; its contents were never published.
timeline.problem_solved: Formalising the alliance with Assad.
timeline.did_it_survive: No: void in practice when Assad fell in December 2024 and Iran did not intervene.

timeline.name: UN Security Council Resolution 1701
timeline.line: Resolution 1701 ends the 2006 war and bars armed men other than the army and UNIFIL south of the Litani
timeline.description: It called for a full cessation of hostilities, an area between the Blue Line and the Litani free of any weapons other than those of the Lebanese state and UNIFIL, and 'no weapons or authority in Lebanon other than that of the Lebanese State'. UNIFIL was enlarged to up to 15,000 troops.
timeline.immediate_effect: Seventeen years of relative quiet on the border.
timeline.long_term_effect: Still the reference text; the 2024 cessation and the 2026 framework are both framed as implementing it.

timeline.name: US Treasury designates the IRGC Quds Force
timeline.line: Treasury names the Quds Force as the supplier of Hezbollah, Hamas and PIJ
timeline.description: The designation under E.O. 13224 cited material support to the Taliban, Lebanese Hizballah, Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad and the PFLP-GC.
timeline.immediate_effect: Financial isolation of the Quds Force network.
timeline.long_term_effect: The first official US document to treat the axis as a single supply system.

timeline.name: Killing of Imad Mughniyeh in Damascus
timeline.line: Hezbollah's military chief is killed; no retaliation is clearly attributed
timeline.description: A car bomb killed Mughniyeh. The Washington Post reported in 2015 that it was a CIA-Mossad operation; Israel denied involvement at the time. The sources used here record no attributed retaliation, so the case is coded not_implemented with low confidence.
timeline.immediate_effect: Loss of the network's senior operator.
timeline.long_term_effect: None attributable in the sources used.

timeline.name: Hezbollah seizes West Beirut; Doha Agreement
timeline.line: Hezbollah turns its guns inward when the cabinet moves on its telecom network
timeline.description: After the government moved to dismantle Hezbollah's private telecom network, Hezbollah and its allies took West Beirut in early May 2008. The Doha Agreement (21 May) gave the opposition a blocking third in cabinet and banned the use of weapons in political disputes.
timeline.immediate_effect: Hezbollah gained a veto over the cabinet.
timeline.long_term_effect: Showed that state moves against Hezbollah's military infrastructure can trigger internal force; that fear shaped the 2025-26 disarmament debate.

timeline.name: Doha Agreement (Lebanon)
timeline.line: Doha ends the May 2008 clashes and gives Hezbollah's camp a cabinet veto
timeline.description: Provided for Sleiman's election, a 16-11-3 cabinet, the 1960 electoral law, and a ban on using weapons in political disputes.
timeline.problem_solved: Stopping intra-Lebanese fighting.
timeline.did_it_survive: Partly: the formula shaped cabinets until 2025.

timeline.name: US designates Kataib Hezbollah and Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis
timeline.line: Kataib Hezbollah is listed as a terrorist organisation; Muhandis is named as Soleimani's adviser
timeline.description: State designated KH an FTO and Treasury designated it and Muhandis for threatening Iraq's stability.
timeline.immediate_effect: Legal basis for later US strikes and sanctions.
timeline.long_term_effect: KH remains the axis's most US-hostile Iraqi faction.

timeline.name: Syrian civil war
timeline.line: Iran, Hezbollah and Russia keep Assad in power for thirteen years, then cannot save him
timeline.description: Iran and Hezbollah intervened from 2012-13 and Russia from 2015. Assad fell on 8 December 2024 to an HTS-led offensive, when Hezbollah had been battered by Israel and Russia was committed in Ukraine.
timeline.immediate_effect: The axis lost its only Arab state member and its land bridge.
timeline.long_term_effect: Syria now interdicts Hezbollah supply.

timeline.name: Hamas leaves Damascus over the Syrian uprising
timeline.line: Hamas breaks with Assad; Iranian funding is cut
timeline.description: Hamas refused to back Assad's crackdown and moved its leadership out of Syria. ECFR reports that Iran cut its funding from about $150m to under $75m. Relations with Damascus were restored when Khalil al-Hayya visited on 19 October 2022.
timeline.immediate_effect: The Sunni partner split from the axis over a Sunni-majority uprising.
timeline.long_term_effect: Evidence that the axis is a set of conditional partnerships, not a command chain.

timeline.name: Hezbollah fights openly for Assad at Qusayr
timeline.line: Nasrallah declares Syria 'our battle'; Hezbollah and the Syrian army retake Qusayr
timeline.description: In a 25 May 2013 speech Nasrallah acknowledged that Hezbollah was fighting in Syria. Qusayr fell to Syrian and Hezbollah forces on 5-6 June.
timeline.immediate_effect: Assad's corridor to Lebanon was secured.
timeline.long_term_effect: Hezbollah became a regional expeditionary force, losing its image as a purely anti-Israel 'resistance' among many Sunnis.

timeline.name: Sistani's call to arms and the rise of the PMF
timeline.line: After Mosul falls, Sistani's call to arms creates the Popular Mobilization Forces
timeline.description: After ISIS took Mosul on 10 June 2014, Sistani's representative called on able citizens to volunteer (a wajib kifa'i). Existing Iran-backed factions led the resulting PMF. Some sources date the call 14 June.
timeline.immediate_effect: Mass mobilisation against ISIS with Quds Force advisers.
timeline.long_term_effect: Iran-aligned factions gained state salaries and legal cover (the 2016 PMF law).

timeline.name: Houthis take Sanaa
timeline.line: The Houthis seize the capital; Hadi resigns in January 2015
timeline.description: The Houthis took government sites in Sanaa as the UN-brokered Peace and National Partnership Agreement was signed. Hadi resigned on 22 January 2015, and a Houthi 'constitutional declaration' dissolved parliament on 6 February 2015. The Houthis call it a revolution; the UN and the government call it a coup.
timeline.immediate_effect: The Houthis controlled the state apparatus in the north.
timeline.long_term_effect: Gave the axis a territorial base on the Red Sea.

timeline.name: Saudi-led intervention in Yemen and UNSCR 2216
timeline.line: Saudi Arabia leads a coalition war on the Houthis; the UN imposes an arms embargo on them
timeline.description: Operation Decisive Storm began on 26 March 2015. UNSCR 2216 (14 April, 14-0, Russia abstaining) imposed an arms embargo on the Houthi leadership and demanded their withdrawal.
timeline.immediate_effect: A seven-year war that did not dislodge the Houthis.
timeline.long_term_effect: Legal frame for arms interdictions; the Saudi-Houthi front reopened in 2026.

timeline.name: Yemen war (Houthis vs the government and the Saudi-led coalition)
timeline.line: A war the Houthis survived, which reopened in 2026
timeline.description: Coalition intervention from 2015, the Stockholm Agreement in 2018 and a truce in 2022 did not settle the war. Fighting with Saudi Arabia resumed in July 2026.
timeline.immediate_effect: Humanitarian catastrophe; Houthi control of the north.
timeline.long_term_effect: Ongoing.

timeline.name: Russian military intervention in Syria
timeline.line: Russian airpower joins Iranian and Hezbollah ground forces to save Assad
timeline.description: Russia began airstrikes on 30 September 2015. Reuters reported that Soleimani visited Moscow in July 2015 to plan it; that account rests on anonymous sources.
timeline.immediate_effect: Turned the war in Assad's favour.
timeline.long_term_effect: Assad's survival came to depend on patrons who both left in 2024 when their own wars stretched them.

timeline.name: Iraq's PMF law
timeline.line: Iraq makes the PMF a legal corps under the commander-in-chief
timeline.description: Law No. 40 of 2016 made the PMF a formal security body. Sunni MPs boycotted the vote.
timeline.immediate_effect: State salaries and legal status for Iran-aligned factions.
timeline.long_term_effect: Factions are inside the state and outside its control; a 2025 bill to expand the PMF was withdrawn under US pressure.

timeline.name: UN Panel finds Iranian-origin missiles in Yemen
timeline.line: UN experts trace missile remnants and drones in Yemen to Iran
timeline.description: The Panel of Experts (S/2018/68) found missile remnants and drones of Iranian origin brought into Yemen after the embargo. Later interdictions include the January 2024 dhow seizure, in which two US Navy SEALs were lost. Iran denies arming the Houthis.
timeline.immediate_effect: Iran was found in non-compliance with the embargo.
timeline.long_term_effect: The documented supply relationship; how much control it brings is disputed.

timeline.name: Stockholm Agreement (Yemen)
timeline.line: Stockholm freezes the battle for Hodeidah
timeline.description: Covered Hodeidah and its ports, a prisoner exchange and Taiz.
timeline.problem_solved: Averting an assault on Hodeidah.
timeline.did_it_survive: Partly; Hodeidah stayed in Houthi hands and became a target of Israeli strikes from 2024.

timeline.name: K1 attack, US strikes on Kataib Hezbollah and the Baghdad embassy siege
timeline.line: A US contractor is killed; US strikes kill 25 KH fighters; militia supporters storm the US embassy
timeline.description: About 30 rockets hit K1 in Kirkuk on 27 December. US strikes on 29 December hit five KH sites and killed 25. On 31 December PMF and KH supporters stormed the embassy compound. Days later the US killed Soleimani and Muhandis.
timeline.immediate_effect: Led directly to the 3 January 2020 strike.
timeline.long_term_effect: Set the pattern of militia rockets followed by US strikes on KH.

timeline.name: Iraqi parliament votes to end foreign troop presence
timeline.line: After Soleimani and Muhandis are killed, parliament calls for foreign forces to leave
timeline.description: A non-binding resolution, boycotted by Sunni and Kurdish MPs, called on the government to end the presence of foreign troops.
timeline.immediate_effect: Political pressure on the US presence.
timeline.long_term_effect: Led to the September 2024 agreement to end the coalition mission in Iraq by September 2025.

timeline.name: 'Unity of the arenas' becomes axis doctrine
timeline.line: The axis starts speaking of 'unity of the arenas': any front can activate the others
timeline.description: Al-Zaytouna traces the idea to the May 2021 Gaza fighting. PIJ named its August 2022 round after it, and Nasrallah later articulated it as strategy. Michael Young argues his 3 November 2023 speech exposed its limits.
timeline.immediate_effect: Rhetorical deterrence based on multiple fronts.
timeline.long_term_effect: The benchmark against which each member's entry or abstention in 2023-2026 is read.

timeline.name: UN-brokered Yemen truce and Saudi-Houthi talks
timeline.line: A truce ends large-scale Saudi-Houthi fighting; a Houthi delegation visits Riyadh in 2023
timeline.description: A two-month truce took effect on 2 April 2022 and largely held after it formally lapsed. A Houthi delegation made its first official visit to Riyadh in September 2023, and the UN announced roadmap commitments in December 2023, never signed.
timeline.immediate_effect: The Saudi front went quiet.
timeline.long_term_effect: Freed Houthi capacity for the Red Sea campaign; the unsigned roadmap left the war unresolved until it reignited in 2026.

timeline.name: Hezbollah opens a 'support front' for Gaza
timeline.line: The day after 7 October, Hezbollah fires on Shebaa 'in solidarity' and holds a calibrated front for eleven months
timeline.description: Hezbollah struck three posts in the Shebaa Farms on 8 October 2023 and kept up cross-border fire short of all-out war until Israel escalated in September 2024. That escalation is coded separately as case:2024_lebanon_war.
timeline.immediate_effect: Tens of thousands displaced on both sides of the border.
timeline.long_term_effect: Calibrated entry did not prevent the 2024 decapitation.

timeline.name: Iraqi factions attack US forces over Gaza
timeline.line: At least 165 attacks on US forces end once Tower 22 kills three Americans
timeline.description: The 'Islamic Resistance in Iraq' attacked US forces in Iraq, Syria and Jordan. After Tower 22 (28 January 2024), KH suspended operations, and US strikes on 85 targets followed.
timeline.immediate_effect: Attacks largely stopped from February 2024.
timeline.long_term_effect: The factions stayed out in June 2025 and returned in 2026.

timeline.name: Houthi Red Sea campaign
timeline.line: The Houthis seize Galaxy Leader and keep attacking shipping through two US air campaigns
timeline.description: The campaign began with the seizure of Galaxy Leader and sank the Rubymar and Tutor (2024), then the Magic Seas and Eternity C (July 2025, after the US truce). It absorbed Poseidon Archer and Rough Rider; the US-Houthi truce of 6 May 2025 covered only US ships.
timeline.immediate_effect: Global shipping rerouted around the Cape.
timeline.long_term_effect: The strongest evidence that a small member can impose global costs on its own terms.

timeline.name: UNSCR 2722 and the first US-UK strikes on the Houthis
timeline.line: The Security Council demands an end to Red Sea attacks; US and UK aircraft strike Yemen
timeline.description: UNSCR 2722 (10 January, 11-0 with four abstentions) demanded that the Houthis stop attacking shipping. US-UK strikes hit about 60 targets on 11-12 January. The US designated the Houthis an SDGT on 17 January, effective 16 February.
timeline.immediate_effect: Attacks continued; ships were later sunk (Rubymar, Tutor).
timeline.long_term_effect: Airstrikes alone did not end the campaign.

timeline.name: Kataib Hezbollah suspends attacks after Tower 22
timeline.line: After killing three US soldiers, KH halts attacks 'so as not to embarrass' Baghdad
timeline.description: After at least 165 attacks on US forces since October 2023 and the 28 January Tower 22 strike, KH announced a suspension. The US still struck 85 targets in Iraq and Syria on 2 February.
timeline.immediate_effect: Iraqi attacks on US forces largely stopped.
timeline.long_term_effect: A case of a faction stepping back once US deaths raised the cost.

timeline.name: Pager attacks and the killing of Nasrallah
timeline.line: Exploding pagers maim Hezbollah's ranks; ten days later Israel kills Nasrallah
timeline.description: Pagers and radios exploded on 17-18 September, killing 37 and wounding more than 2,900 (AFP); the attack was widely attributed to Israel. Nasrallah was killed in a strike on Dahiyeh on 27 September, and Naim Qassem was named Secretary-General on 29 October.
timeline.immediate_effect: Hezbollah's command was decapitated and an Israeli ground operation followed.
timeline.long_term_effect: Hezbollah accepted the November 2024 cessation; Lebanon's state gained room to push disarmament.

timeline.name: US-Iraq timeline to end the coalition mission
timeline.line: The coalition mission in Iraq is set to end by September 2025, in Syria by September 2026
timeline.description: A joint statement set the end of the coalition's military mission in federal Iraq 'no later than the end of September 2025'.
timeline.immediate_effect: Met a core militia demand.
timeline.long_term_effect: US forces still in the region were targeted by Iraqi factions in 2026.

timeline.name: Israel-Lebanon cessation of hostilities
timeline.line: A US-French brokered ceasefire: the army deploys south, Israel withdraws within 60 days, only state forces may bear arms
timeline.description: Effective 27 November 2024. The published text commits Lebanon to prevent attacks by Hezbollah, limits arms to official forces, sets a 60-day Israeli withdrawal and creates a US-chaired monitoring mechanism. It preserves both sides' 'inherent right of self-defense'. A reported US side letter on Israeli freedom of action is unconfirmed.
timeline.problem_solved: Ending the 2023-24 war.
timeline.did_it_survive: No: Israeli strikes continued throughout (e.g. Tabatabai, November 2025) and full war resumed on 2 March 2026.

timeline.name: The axis does not rescue Assad
timeline.line: Iran and Hezbollah, who fought for Assad for a decade, do not move to save him in December 2024
timeline.description: The HTS-led offensive reached Damascus in under two weeks. Hezbollah, just out of its war with Israel, and Iran did not mount a rescue despite the 2006 defence pact. Al-Sharaa later said the axis's project had been 'set back 40 years'.
timeline.immediate_effect: Assad fell on 8 December 2024.
timeline.long_term_effect: Loss of the land bridge.

timeline.name: Joseph Aoun elected president of Lebanon
timeline.line: Lebanon ends a two-year vacancy with a president pledged to a state monopoly of arms
timeline.description: The army commander was elected with 99 of 128 votes and pledged to confirm 'the state's right to monopolise the carrying of weapons'.
timeline.immediate_effect: The first head of state in decades to make disarmament his programme.
timeline.long_term_effect: Led to the August 2025 cabinet decision.

timeline.name: US redesignates the Houthis a Foreign Terrorist Organization
timeline.line: Trump reverses Biden's 2021 delisting and names Ansar Allah an FTO
timeline.description: E.O. 14175 (22 January 2025) ordered the redesignation; State announced it on 4 March and it took effect on 5 March. Biden had revoked the first FTO listing in 2021.
timeline.immediate_effect: Material-support liability for dealings in Houthi areas.
timeline.long_term_effect: Followed within weeks by Operation Rough Rider.

timeline.name: Oman-mediated US-Houthi truce
timeline.line: The US and the Houthis agree not to target each other; Israel is not covered
timeline.description: Oman announced that 'neither side will target the other, including U.S. vessels', ending the 52-day Operation Rough Rider.
timeline.problem_solved: Ending US-Houthi fighting.
timeline.did_it_survive: As far as the sources show, the Houthis did not attack US ships while striking Israel (2025) and Saudi Arabia (2026).

timeline.name: The axis stays out of the June 2025 Israel-Iran war
timeline.line: When Iran itself is struck, Hezbollah and the Iraqi factions do not fire
timeline.description: WINEP found 'no evidence yet' of Iraqi militia strikes on US forces, and PM Sudani said Iraqi forces stopped 29 attempted attacks. Hezbollah did not open a front.
timeline.immediate_effect: Iran fought alone.
timeline.long_term_effect: Undercut the 'unity of arenas' deterrent, which was then applied in 2026.

timeline.name: US lifts the Syria sanctions programme
timeline.line: Washington ends the Syria sanctions regime while keeping sanctions on Iran's proxies
timeline.description: E.O. 14312 terminated the Syria national emergency from 1 July 2025, keeping measures on Assad associates, ISIS, and Iran and its proxies.
timeline.immediate_effect: Anchored the post-Assad government in the Western and Gulf camp.
timeline.long_term_effect: Syria went from the axis's hub to a state that interdicts it.

timeline.name: Lebanese cabinet orders a state monopoly of arms
timeline.line: Lebanon's cabinet tasks the army with disarming Hezbollah; Hezbollah says it will ignore the decision
timeline.description: On 5 August 2025 the cabinet tasked the army with a plan to confine weapons to state forces by year-end; Shia ministers walked out. Hezbollah called it a 'grave sin' and said it would treat it 'as if it does not exist'. The cabinet welcomed the army's plan on 5 September without a timeline.
timeline.immediate_effect: The first formal cabinet decision against Hezbollah's arms.
timeline.long_term_effect: Set up the March 2026 ban and the June 2026 framework.

timeline.name: Iraq withdraws the PMF bill under US pressure
timeline.line: Baghdad shelves a law that would have entrenched the PMF
timeline.description: After Secretary Rubio pressed Baghdad, the government withdrew the bill.
timeline.immediate_effect: The PMF's legal expansion stalled.
timeline.long_term_effect: Baghdad later set 30 September 2026 as the deadline for placing all weapons under state control.

timeline.name: Israel kills the Houthi prime minister and ministers
timeline.line: An Israeli strike in Sanaa kills PM al-Rahawi; the chief of staff's death is announced in October
timeline.description: The Houthis confirmed that Ahmed al-Rahawi and several ministers were killed; on 16 October they announced chief of staff al-Ghamari's death, which Israel claimed. Houthi fire on Israel continued in the same period.
timeline.immediate_effect: No change in Houthi behaviour.
timeline.long_term_effect: Decapitation did not stop the Houthis.

timeline.name: Israel kills Hezbollah chief of staff Tabatabai in Beirut
timeline.line: A year into the ceasefire, Israel kills Hezbollah's military chief; Hezbollah does not answer until the Iran war
timeline.description: The Haret Hreik strike killed at least five. The sources used record no Hezbollah military response before Hezbollah entered the war on 2 March 2026 (Qassem's response speech was not sourced).
timeline.immediate_effect: Hezbollah absorbed the strike.
timeline.long_term_effect: Hezbollah fired only when Iran itself was at war.

timeline.name: Iraqi factions join the 2026 war
timeline.line: From day one, Iraqi factions launch hundreds of drone and missile attacks, including on the US embassy
timeline.description: The factions claimed 100+ attacks by 20 March and 300+ by mid-March by other counts (their own claims). US and other strikes killed 60+ PMF fighters. KH declared a conditional pause on embassy attacks on 19 March, and on 7 August the factions postponed retaliation against Saudi Arabia. A drone from Maysan shut the Saudi East-West pipeline around 11 September.
timeline.immediate_effect: The Iraqi front stayed active but was interrupted by pauses.
timeline.long_term_effect: Baghdad's 30 September 2026 weapons deadline.

timeline.name: Lebanon bans Hezbollah's military activity as Hezbollah joins the Iran war
timeline.line: Hezbollah fires on Israel for Iran; the same day Lebanon's government bans its military activity
timeline.description: Hezbollah fired at a missile-defence site near Haifa on 2 March, and Israeli strikes the same day killed at least 52. PM Salam's cabinet banned Hezbollah military activity, restricting it 'to the political sphere'. Hezbollah fired again the next day.
timeline.immediate_effect: Hezbollah in open defiance of its own government.
timeline.long_term_effect: The legal break between the Lebanese state and the 'resistance'.

timeline.name: Hezbollah joins the 2026 war on Iran's side
timeline.line: Two days after Khamenei is killed, Hezbollah fires on Haifa in defiance of its own government
timeline.description: Hezbollah entered on 2 March 2026 despite its 2024 losses and a same-day Lebanese government ban. Israel answered with a large campaign. Pakistan said the April ceasefire covered Lebanon; Netanyahu said it did not. Low-level fighting continued after the June framework.
timeline.immediate_effect: A renewed Israel-Lebanon war.
timeline.long_term_effect: Disarmament is now tied to Israeli withdrawal (June 2026 framework).

timeline.name: Hamas and PIJ stay out of the 2026 war
timeline.line: Hamas says Gaza's devastation rules out a support front for Iran, and asks Iran to stop hitting the Gulf
timeline.description: ITIC reported that the Palestinian groups would not open a front because of the damage from the Gaza war. On 14 March Hamas urged 'the brothers in Iran' to avoid targeting neighbouring countries.
timeline.immediate_effect: No Gaza front.
timeline.long_term_effect: The member that started the 2023 cycle sat out the war on its patron.

timeline.name: The Houthis enter the 2026 war after a month
timeline.line: The Houthis wait a month, then fire at Israel; from July they turn on Saudi Arabia
timeline.description: The first 2026 missiles at Israel were fired on 28 March, with a threat to close Bab el-Mandeb. Security Council Report found no merchant-ship attacks in 2026 as of July and none after the June MOU. From July the Houthis fought Saudi Arabia (event:2026_saudi_houthi_war).
timeline.immediate_effect: A late, limited entry.
timeline.long_term_effect: The front shifted from Israel to Saudi Arabia.

timeline.name: Ali al-Zaidi's government wins confidence
timeline.line: Iraq forms a Coordination Framework government with defence and interior left vacant
timeline.description: Parliament approved 14 of 23 ministers; the security ministries stayed open.
timeline.immediate_effect: A new PM facing the militia-weapons question.
timeline.long_term_effect: The 30 September 2026 weapons deadline falls on this government.

timeline.name: Israel-Lebanon framework (Washington)
timeline.line: Israel and Lebanon tie Israeli withdrawal to Hezbollah's disarmament
timeline.description: Signed in Washington. In August the parties agreed on countries that could verify disarmament. Qassem called it 'a very dangerous proposition that crosses all red lines'; low-level fighting continues.
timeline.problem_solved: Converting the war into a disarmament-for-withdrawal track.
timeline.did_it_survive: Pending as of September 2026.

timeline.name: The Saudi-Houthi war reopens
timeline.line: The Houthis end their 'de-escalation phase' with Saudi Arabia, blockade it and push down the Red Sea coast
timeline.description: After a 13 July strike on Sanaa airport blocked an Iranian plane (attributed by some to Yemen's government, by others to Saudi Arabia), the Houthis fired on Saudi Arabia. They declared a maritime blockade on 20 July, hit Aramco sites, and in September advanced on Mocha, Dhubab, Perim and the Hanish islands. On 15-16 September a drone was intercepted near Mecca (the Houthis deny targeting the city) and they claimed a Saudi F-15 shot down (unverified). The drone that shut the East-West pipeline around 11 September came from Iraq, not Yemen.
timeline.immediate_effect: Saudi Arabia is under attack from two axis directions while Hormuz is disrupted.
timeline.long_term_effect: Unresolved; ends the 2022 truce.

timeline.name: Syria seizes weapons bound for Hezbollah
timeline.line: Damascus intercepts missiles, rockets and drones headed for Hezbollah
timeline.description: Syrian authorities said they seized missiles, rockets and drones bound for Hezbollah at al-Tanf. Hezbollah denied it, and Iraq opened an inquiry.
timeline.immediate_effect: Confirmed that the land corridor is now hostile ground.
timeline.long_term_effect: Hezbollah's rearmament depends on routes Iran no longer controls.

timeline.name: Drone from Iraq shuts Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline
timeline.line: An unclaimed drone launched from Iraq's Maysan province shuts the Hormuz bypass pipeline
timeline.description: Saudi Arabia shut the pipeline after a drone attack traced to Maysan province. No group claimed it; attribution to Iraqi factions is an assessment, and one analyst suggested Tehran ordered it.
timeline.immediate_effect: The Hormuz bypass went offline.
timeline.long_term_effect: Iraqi factions are now a threat to Gulf energy, not just to US bases.

territories.name: Shebaa Farms

current_claims.basis: Lebanon, backed by Syria in statements, says the farms are Lebanese
The UN line treats the area as Syrian territory occupied in 1967

territories.recognition: In 2000 the UN used the UNDOF/UNIFIL line, which places the farms on the Golan side, 'without prejudice' to a future Lebanon-Syria border agreement.
significance: Hezbollah's stated reason for continued 'resistance' after the 2000 withdrawal
the first targets of the 8 October 2023 support front

territories.name: South Lebanon (Blue Line to the Litani)

historical_control.note: Israeli 'security zone' with the South Lebanon Army (start date approximate)
de facto armed presence alongside LAF and UNIFIL after 2006
LAF deployment under the cessation of hostilities; Israeli forces kept positions and strikes continue

current_claims.basis: sovereign Lebanese territory

territories.recognition: Universally recognised as Lebanese. Resolution 1701 requires the area to be free of armed personnel other than the LAF and UNIFIL.
territories.de_facto_control: contested: LAF, with Israeli forces holding positions and fighting since March 2026
significance: Hezbollah's rocket launch zone
the core of every disarmament text since 2006

territories.name: Houthi-held northern Yemen (Sanaa, Saada, Hodeidah)

current_claims.basis: the internationally recognised government (Presidential Leadership Council) claims all Yemen
the Supreme Political Council (2016) presents itself as Yemen's government

territories.recognition: No UN member state other than Iran has treated the Houthi authorities as Yemen's government. UNSCR 2216 demands a Houthi withdrawal.
significance: Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb coastline
launch area against Israel and Saudi Arabia

lessons.name: Iran: support for the 'mustad'afun' is constitutional; the partners are declared autonomous
lessons.description: Article 154 commits Iran to support 'the just struggles of the mustad'afun against the mustakbirun', and the preamble gives the armed forces an 'ideological mission of jihad'. Khamenei said in December 2024 that 'the Islamic Republic does not have a proxy force'. The doctrine is written; whether the partners are in fact autonomous is a separate, empirical question.

lessons.name: Each member decides its own entry into a war, on its own clock
lessons.description: Scholars such as the Sana'a Center and ECFR describe the network as conditional partnerships rather than a command chain. The record fits: Hamas left Damascus in 2012; the axis sat out June 2025; in 2026 Hezbollah joined on day 3, the Houthis on day 29 and Hamas not at all.

lessons.name: Lebanon: disarmament texts go unimplemented until the military balance changes
lessons.description: Taif (1989), 1559 (2004) and 1701 (2006) all required disarmament and none was applied to Hezbollah. The state acted (2025 decision, 2026 ban) only after Israel had killed Hezbollah's leadership and Assad had fallen, and it still ties implementation to Israeli withdrawal.

lessons.name: Killing leaders has not ended any axis member
lessons.description: Musawi was replaced by Nasrallah (1992), Hussein al-Houthi by Abdul-Malik (2004), Soleimani by Qaani (2020), Nasrallah by Qassem (2024), and Houthi fire continued after al-Rahawi was killed (2025). Decapitation changed capability and timing, not existence. The claim is an inference from a small set.

lessons.name: Hezbollah's strength depends on who rules Damascus
lessons.description: Hezbollah fought for Assad because Syria was its supply line. After December 2024, Damascus began seizing weapons bound for Hezbollah (July 2026).

lessons.name: Hezbollah: its own leader said the 2006 escalation was a miscalculation
lessons.description: Nasrallah said on 27 August 2006 that he would 'absolutely not' have ordered the abduction had he known it would lead to war. It is on the record, and the calibrated 2006-2023 border fits it; it is not a written doctrine.

tendencies.name: Axis members join a patron's or partner's war selectively, weighing their own survival
current_evidence: In 2026 Hezbollah and the Iraqi factions entered at once, the Houthis after a month, Hamas never; Iraqi factions paused embassy attacks in March and postponed retaliation on Saudi Arabia in August.
tendencies.caveat: The killing of the Supreme Leader in 2026 may have been a threshold that the June 2025 strikes were not; with n this small, 'selective' may simply mean 'depends on the size of the blow to Iran'.

tendencies.name: Hezbollah refuses to give up its arms, framing them as national resistance
current_evidence: Qassem, August 2025: 'We will not abandon the weapons that honour us'; June 2026 framework called a proposition that 'crosses all red lines'.
tendencies.caveat: Hezbollah accepted a south-of-Litani arrangement in 2024 and a ban on internal use of weapons in 2008; it trades position, not the principle. A leadership further weakened or cut off from Iran could accept more.

tendencies.name: The Houthis absorb military pressure and keep firing, but take deals that exclude their chosen target
current_evidence: After the May 2025 truce with the US, fire continued at Israel; in 2026 the Houthis delayed entry a month, then opened a Saudi front in July.
tendencies.caveat: Truces in 2022 and 2025 show that the Houthis bargain; the resilience may reflect terrain and a lack of ground pressure rather than a fixed culture.

path_dependencies.name: From Taif's exemption to the 2026 disarmament-for-withdrawal track

chain.step: 1982-85 Hezbollah founded with IRGC help; allegiance to the faqih
1989 Taif disarms militias; Hezbollah keeps arms as 'resistance'
2000 withdrawal; Shebaa gives a continuing rationale
2006 war; 1701 bars arms south of the Litani, unimplemented
2023 support front; 2024 decapitation
2024 Assad falls; supply line lost
2025 cabinet decision; 2026 ban and Washington framework
Current constraint: disarmament is formally state policy but tied to Israeli withdrawal, while Hezbollah fights on

path_dependencies.description: The arrows are hypotheses about causation; the documents and events are sourced, their causal weight is an assessment.

path_dependencies.name: From Badr in exile to militias inside the Iraqi state

chain.step: 1982 Badr raised by the IRGC in Iran
2003 US invasion lets Iran-aligned exiles return
2014 Sistani's call to arms creates the PMF
2016 PMF law makes the factions state bodies
2019-20 embassy crisis, Soleimani and Muhandis killed, expulsion vote
2023-26 factions attack US forces, pause, resume
Current constraint: factions are paid by the state they defy; the 30 September 2026 weapons deadline tests which way that runs

path_dependencies.description: The arrows are hypotheses; each step is documented, the causal links are an assessment.

narratives.name: 'Resistance', not proxies: whose war is it?
narratives.historical_event: Iran's support for the groups since 1982; the Quds Force supply record (Treasury 2007, UN Panel 2018).
narratives.modern_interpretation: Tehran says the members fight 'because they have faith' and that it has no proxies (Khamenei, December 2024). US and Israeli officials call them Iranian proxies. Scholars split: the Sana'a Center says the Houthis are 'best not viewed as a proxy'; Johnsen reads their 2026 entry as confirming 'loyalty and value to Iran'. The documented record shows supply and coordination, and repeated instances of members deciding for themselves.

narratives.name: Hezbollah: resistance liberated the south and its weapons protect Lebanon
narratives.historical_event: Israel's May 2000 withdrawal from south Lebanon.
narratives.modern_interpretation: Hezbollah presents 2000 as proof that arms, not diplomacy, freed Lebanese land, and grounds its refusal to disarm in the continued occupation of Shebaa and Israeli strikes. The 2009 Political Document calls the resistance 'a national necessity'; Qassem in 2025 spoke of weapons 'that protect us from our enemy'. Its opponents in Lebanon answer that the arms invited the 2006, 2024 and 2026 wars.

narratives.name: Who bombed Buenos Aires (1992, 1994)?
narratives.historical_event: The 1992 embassy and 1994 AMIA bombings.
narratives.modern_interpretation: Argentina's Cassation court (April 2024) attributes both to Iran and Hezbollah. Iran calls the ruling politically motivated and 'baseless', and Hezbollah denies involvement. The court record is the main source; decades of investigative irregularities in Argentina are part of why the attribution is still contested abroad.

narratives.name: Did Iran know about 7 October?
narratives.historical_event: The Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023.
narratives.modern_interpretation: Khamenei praised the planners ('we kiss the hands') while denying Iranian involvement. Early US intelligence (October 2023) found Iranian officials surprised, and an ODNI assessment of February 2024 (quoted by CRS) said Iranian leaders neither orchestrated nor had foreknowledge of it. Other press reporting claimed Iranian approval in Beirut; that reporting was not verified for this file.

asymmetric_rocket_conflict_round.selection_note: Cases are named Israeli military operations or wars against a non-state armed group that fires rockets or missiles from adjacent territory (Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad in Gaza, Hezbollah in Lebanon), 2006-2024. The set is the named rounds only: it omits the hundreds of smaller exchanges that ended within a day and the 2000-2005 intifada (a different form of conflict). 'limited_conflict' means a bounded round ended by a mediated or unilateral ceasefire with the group still governing or armed; 'war' means ground invasion aimed at removing or crippling the group. Famous rounds are over-represented relative to quiet periods, so the set says how rounds END, not how often they START. The 2023-25 Gaza war and the 2024 Lebanon war broke the earlier 'bounded round' pattern; weight post-October 2023 cases accordingly.
