why_it_matters.line: US and Israel launch a war on Iran that kills Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei; Iran strikes Israel and Gulf states hosting US forces

why_it_matters.name: Iran blocks Hormuz and imposes a permit-and-toll regime
why_it_matters.line: For the first time Iran actually closes the strait, then runs it through a permit and toll authority

why_it_matters.name: US-Iran Memorandum of Understanding of 17 June 2026
why_it_matters.line: 14-point MOU halts hostilities and sets a 60-day window for a final deal on Hormuz, the nuclear program and sanctions

timeline.name: Pahlavi Iran extends de facto recognition to Israel
timeline.line: The Shah's Iran quietly recognizes Israel, beginning three decades of covert partnership
timeline.description: Iran granted Israel de facto recognition without formal embassies. The relationship grew into security, intelligence and oil cooperation under Israel's 'periphery' strategy of aligning with non-Arab states.
timeline.immediate_effect: Unofficial Israeli mission in Tehran.
timeline.long_term_effect: Ended in February 1979 when the revolutionary government cut ties; its existence shows Iran-Israel enmity is a product of the 1979 regime, not of geography or national identity.

timeline.name: Coup against Prime Minister Mossadegh
timeline.line: US- and UK-backed coup removes Mossadegh after oil nationalization
timeline.description: After Iran nationalized the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, a CIA- and MI6-supported operation restored the Shah's authority. The CIA acknowledged its role in documents released in 2013.
timeline.immediate_effect: Shah consolidated power; oil consortium with Western majors.
timeline.long_term_effect: A documented grievance central to the Islamic Republic's narrative of foreign interference.

timeline.name: US-Iran Treaty of Amity, Economic Relations, and Consular Rights
timeline.line: Pahlavi-era commercial treaty that outlived the revolution until the US terminated it in 2018
timeline.description: A standard friendship and commerce treaty signed with the Shah's government. It survived the 1979 break and became the jurisdictional basis for Iranian cases against the US at the ICJ. On 3 October 2018, the day the ICJ ordered provisional measures in Iran's sanctions case, the US gave notice of termination, effective one year later.
timeline.problem_solved: Commercial and consular relations with a Cold War ally.
timeline.did_it_survive: Nominally survived 1979 for four decades, used mainly as a litigation vehicle; terminated by the US with effect from 2019.

timeline.name: Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons
timeline.line: Iran signs the NPT in 1968; Israel never joins
timeline.description: Pahlavi Iran signed on the opening day and ratified in 1970; the Islamic Republic inherited the obligation and its IAEA safeguards agreement. Israel is not a party and maintains a policy of nuclear opacity. Iranian officials have periodically threatened withdrawal.
timeline.problem_solved: Limiting the spread of nuclear weapons in exchange for access to civilian nuclear technology.
timeline.did_it_survive: In force for Iran as of September 2026, but IAEA verification in Iran was largely suspended after mid-2025; the Board found Iran in non-compliance in 2005 and 2025.

timeline.name: Iranian Revolution and embassy seizure
timeline.line: Revolution replaces the monarchy; US embassy seized in November
timeline.description: The Pahlavi monarchy fell in February 1979; the Islamic Republic was proclaimed in April; the US embassy was seized on 4 November and 52 hostages held for 444 days.
timeline.immediate_effect: Rupture of US-Iran relations that has never been repaired.
timeline.long_term_effect: Sanctions architecture, US regional basing and Iran's 'resistance' posture all descend from this break.

timeline.name: Algiers Accords
timeline.line: Algerian mediation ends the hostage crisis; the US pledges non-intervention in Iran's internal affairs
timeline.description: The 52 hostages were freed on 20 January 1981 in exchange for unfreezing Iranian assets and creating the Iran-US Claims Tribunal in The Hague. Point I of the General Declaration states US policy is not to intervene in Iran's internal affairs.
timeline.problem_solved: Release of the hostages and a mechanism to settle the frozen-asset dispute.
timeline.did_it_survive: The Claims Tribunal still sits; the non-intervention pledge is cited by Iran against US regime-change policy and was plainly overtaken by the 2026 war. No US-Iran diplomatic relations were restored.

timeline.name: Israeli strike on Iraq's Osirak reactor (Operation Opera)
timeline.line: Israeli jets destroy Iraq's French-built reactor before it is fueled; the Security Council condemns the raid
timeline.description: Israeli F-16s destroyed the Osirak (Tammuz 1) reactor near Baghdad. Prime Minister Begin's government said Israel would not allow an enemy to develop weapons of mass destruction against its people. UNSCR 487, supported by the US, strongly condemned the attack. Iraq, already at war with Iran, did not retaliate militarily.
timeline.immediate_effect: No military retaliation; diplomatic condemnation.
timeline.long_term_effect: Braut-Hegghammer's archival study finds the strike turned a loosely organized program into a covert weapons drive; the program was ended by the 1991 war and inspections, not by the raid.

timeline.name: US-Israel Memorandum of Understanding on Strategic Cooperation
timeline.line: First formal US-Israel strategic cooperation agreement, aimed at the Soviet threat
timeline.description: Framed cooperation against Soviet threats in the region. The US suspended it weeks later after Israel's Golan Heights Law of December 1981; cooperation was institutionalized again from 1983 through joint political-military consultations.
timeline.problem_solved: Giving Israel a formal strategic role in US Cold War planning.
timeline.did_it_survive: Suspended almost immediately, but the cooperation it described was rebuilt and deepened; the US-Israel relationship remains an alignment of MOUs and statutes, not a mutual defense treaty.

timeline.name: IRGC helps found Hezbollah in Lebanon
timeline.line: Revolutionary Guards deployed to Lebanon's Bekaa valley help create Hezbollah after Israel's invasion
timeline.description: An IRGC contingent sent to Lebanon after Israel's June 1982 invasion organized, trained and funded Shia militants who became Hezbollah; its 1985 Open Letter declared allegiance to Khomeini's leadership.
timeline.immediate_effect: Iran acquired a force on Israel's northern border.
timeline.long_term_effect: The template for Iran's network of partner forces and for its forward deterrence against Israel, until Hezbollah was badly degraded in 2024.

timeline.name: Bombing of the US Marine barracks in Beirut
timeline.line: Truck bomb kills 241 US service members in Beirut; the US withdraws from Lebanon months later
timeline.description: A suicide truck bomb destroyed the Marine barracks (a simultaneous attack killed 58 French paratroopers). The US attributes it to the group that became Hezbollah acting with Iranian support; a US federal court held Iran liable in 2003. Iran denies involvement.
timeline.immediate_effect: US forces left Lebanon in February 1984.
timeline.long_term_effect: Cemented the US view of Iran as a sponsor of terrorism and the Iranian view that US forces could be driven out by cost.

timeline.name: Iran-Contra arms sales
timeline.line: Reagan administration secretly sells missiles to Iran, initially through Israel, seeking hostages' release
timeline.description: TOW and HAWK missile components were shipped to Iran in 1985-86, the first consignments via Israel, in hopes of freeing US hostages in Lebanon; proceeds were diverted to the Nicaraguan Contras. The Tower Commission documented the operation after it was exposed in November 1986.
timeline.immediate_effect: Political scandal in Washington; a few hostages released while others were taken.
timeline.long_term_effect: Discredited back-channel engagement with Tehran in US politics for a generation, and showed Israel still saw Iran as a counterweight to Iraq in the mid-1980s.

timeline.name: 'A Clean Break' published by the IASPS study group
timeline.line: A private US-Israeli study group publishes the paper that names rolling back Syria and removing Saddam as Israeli objectives
timeline.description: The Institute for Advanced Strategic and Political Studies published a strategy paper written by a study group led by Richard Perle and including Douglas Feith, David and Meyrav Wurmser, James Colbert, Charles Fairbanks Jr. and Robert Loewenberg, addressed to the incoming Netanyahu government. It urged abandoning land-for-peace for 'peace for peace', rolling back Syria, removing Saddam Hussein, and striking Hezbollah, Syria and Iran as the agents of aggression in Lebanon.
timeline.immediate_effect: None as policy: Netanyahu's first government did not adopt it and Israel did not attack Syria.
timeline.long_term_effect: Three of its named participants held or advised US policy offices from 2001. The paper is the earliest dated document in this graph that sets out, in one place, the regional sequence later pursued - Iraq first, then the Iranian axis in Lebanon and Syria. Whether it caused anything is contested; that it was written, by whom, and what it said is not.

timeline.name: Iran and Libya Sanctions Act: secondary sanctions arrive
timeline.line: Congress threatens sanctions on foreign companies that invest in Iranian oil and gas
timeline.description: Public Law 104-172 required sanctions on persons making investments above a threshold that significantly enhanced Iran's ability to develop its petroleum resources, reaching foreign firms outside US jurisdiction.
timeline.immediate_effect: European governments objected; waivers were used.
timeline.long_term_effect: The legal template for every later secondary-sanctions regime against Iran, including the shipping and insurance measures that actually moved Iranian barrels after 2012.

timeline.name: Operation Desert Fox against Iraq's WMD programs
timeline.line: US and UK bomb Iraqi WMD-related sites after Baghdad obstructs inspectors
timeline.description: Four days of US and UK air and missile strikes on facilities associated with weapons programs and the regime's security apparatus after UNSCOM reported Iraqi non-cooperation. Inspectors did not return until late 2002.
timeline.immediate_effect: End of UN inspections in Iraq for four years.
timeline.long_term_effect: Loss of on-the-ground verification fed the intelligence uncertainty that preceded the 2003 invasion.

timeline.name: Bush names Iran in the 'axis of evil'
timeline.line: Bush groups Iran with Iraq and North Korea months after Iran cooperated with the US in Afghanistan
timeline.description: The State of the Union address accused Iran of pursuing weapons of mass destruction and exporting terror, shortly after Iranian diplomats had worked with the US at the Bonn conference on Afghanistan.
timeline.immediate_effect: Reformist government of Khatami weakened in the argument for engagement.
timeline.long_term_effect: Framed Iran as a candidate for the same treatment as Iraq, a reading Iranian leaders invoked for years.

timeline.name: Undeclared Natanz and Arak sites revealed
timeline.line: Exiled opposition reveals secret enrichment and heavy-water sites; IAEA later confirms 18 years of undeclared work
timeline.description: An Iranian opposition group publicized the Natanz enrichment site and the Arak heavy-water facility. The IAEA Director General's November 2003 report found Iran had failed over many years to declare nuclear material and activities.
timeline.immediate_effect: IAEA inspections intensified; E3 diplomacy began.
timeline.long_term_effect: The origin of the nuclear file as an international crisis and of the trust deficit every later negotiation had to overcome.

timeline.name: US-led invasion of Iraq
timeline.line: US invades Iraq on WMD grounds; no stockpiles are found
timeline.description: The invasion was justified largely by claims about Iraqi weapons of mass destruction. The Iraq Survey Group concluded in 2004 that Iraq had no stockpiles and had ended its nuclear program after 1991.
timeline.immediate_effect: Saddam Hussein removed; Iran's main regional enemy eliminated.
timeline.long_term_effect: Gave Iran strategic depth in Iraq and made the WMD intelligence failure the standing caution in US debates over striking Iran.

timeline.name: Tehran Declaration with the E3
timeline.line: Iran agrees with Britain, France and Germany to suspend enrichment and sign the Additional Protocol
timeline.description: Iran agreed to suspend enrichment and cooperate with the IAEA; the arrangement was extended by the 2004 Paris Agreement and ended when Iran resumed uranium conversion in August 2005.
timeline.immediate_effect: Temporary suspension.
timeline.long_term_effect: First demonstration that Iran would pause under pressure plus negotiation, and that pauses were reversible.

timeline.name: IAEA Board finds Iran in non-compliance
timeline.line: IAEA Board declares Iran non-compliant; referral to the Security Council follows in February 2006
timeline.description: Resolution GOV/2005/77 found Iran's past safeguards failures constituted non-compliance; the Board reported Iran to the Security Council in February 2006.
timeline.immediate_effect: Iran ended voluntary implementation of the Additional Protocol.
timeline.long_term_effect: Put the file in the Security Council, where the UN sanctions of 2006-10 were built.

timeline.name: The Security Council imposes nuclear sanctions on Iran
timeline.line: The first UN sanctions over enrichment, followed by four more resolutions to 2010
timeline.description: Resolution 1737 required suspension of enrichment and imposed targeted measures; resolution 1929 in 2010 added shipping inspections and restrictions on Iranian financial institutions.
timeline.immediate_effect: Iran continued enriching and expanded Natanz.
timeline.long_term_effect: Built the multilateral sanctions architecture that the JCPOA lifted in 2016 and the E3 snapback restored in September 2025.

timeline.name: Israeli strike on Syria's al-Kibar reactor
timeline.line: Israel secretly destroys a North Korean-designed reactor in Syria; Syria stays silent
timeline.description: Israeli aircraft destroyed an undeclared plutonium-production reactor under construction near Deir ez-Zor. Israel kept official silence until March 2018; Syria did not retaliate or publicize the loss, and the IAEA later found Syria in non-compliance.
timeline.immediate_effect: No retaliation; deniability helped both sides avoid escalation.
timeline.long_term_effect: Israel's 2018 disclosure explicitly framed the strike as a message about Iran.

timeline.name: US intelligence judges Iran halted weaponization in 2003
timeline.line: US National Intelligence Estimate says Iran halted its nuclear weapons work in fall 2003
timeline.description: The declassified Key Judgments assessed with high confidence that Iran halted its nuclear weaponization program in fall 2003, while continuing enrichment that could later support a weapon. Israeli officials disputed the emphasis, and the archive Israel seized in 2018 documented the scale of the pre-2003 program.
timeline.immediate_effect: Removed the near-term case for US military action against Iran in the Bush administration's final year.
timeline.long_term_effect: The 'halted weaponization but kept the option' reading remains contested and underlies the threshold-state debate.

timeline.name: Brookings publishes the Iran options menu 'Which Path to Persia?'
timeline.line: A Washington think tank lays out the full menu of Iran options, including how an offer refused sets up a strike
timeline.description: The Saban Center at Brookings published a 170-page menu of US options toward Iran - persuasion, containment, sanctions, covert action, support for opposition, an Israeli strike, a US air campaign, invasion - written up with costs. The 'Persuasion' chapter argued that a strike draws least international opprobrium when it follows a superb offer that Iran has publicly refused.
timeline.immediate_effect: None directly; the Obama administration pursued sanctions and then negotiation.
timeline.long_term_effect: The offer-deadline-strike sequence it described is the shape of 2025 and 2026: Oman-mediated talks, a lapsed deadline, then force. The paper is evidence that the logic was explicit in Washington a decade and a half before, not evidence that anyone followed it.

timeline.name: Killings of Iranian nuclear scientists and the 2012 attacks on Israeli diplomats
timeline.line: Four Iranian nuclear scientists are killed in Tehran; bomb attacks target Israeli diplomats abroad in February 2012
timeline.description: Iran blamed Israel for a series of killings of nuclear scientists in 2010-12; Israel did not confirm. In February 2012 bombs targeted Israeli diplomats in New Delhi and Tbilisi, and Iranian nationals were arrested after an explosion in Bangkok. Iranian responsibility for the attacks was asserted by Israel and by Indian and Thai investigations; Iran denied it.
timeline.immediate_effect: Diplomat injured in New Delhi; no escalation between states.
timeline.long_term_effect: Retaliation ran through deniable plots abroad rather than state-on-state strikes.

timeline.name: Stuxnet sabotage of Natanz centrifuges comes to light
timeline.line: A cyberweapon that damaged Natanz centrifuges is discovered
timeline.description: Malware designed to damage centrifuges at Natanz was discovered in 2010. Reporting in 2012 described it as a joint US-Israeli program (Olympic Games) accelerated under Obama; neither government has officially acknowledged it.
timeline.immediate_effect: Setback to Iran's centrifuge operations of disputed size.
timeline.long_term_effect: Established covert sabotage as the preferred middle option between diplomacy and strikes for more than a decade.

timeline.name: UNSCR 1929 and CISADA tighten sanctions
timeline.line: Broadest UN sanctions yet, followed within weeks by the US CISADA law targeting Iran's banking and fuel imports
timeline.description: Resolution 1929 expanded arms and financial restrictions; the Comprehensive Iran Sanctions, Accountability, and Divestment Act (P.L. 111-195, 1 July 2010) extended US secondary sanctions. EU oil and central bank measures followed in 2012.
timeline.immediate_effect: Iran's oil exports and currency fell sharply by 2012-13.
timeline.long_term_effect: The pressure that brought Iran to the 2013 interim deal, and the template for the later maximum-pressure campaigns.

timeline.name: Joint Plan of Action
timeline.line: Interim deal freezes key parts of Iran's program for limited sanctions relief
timeline.description: Negotiated in Geneva after secret US-Iran talks hosted by Oman: Iran capped enrichment at 5 percent and diluted or converted its 20 percent stock in exchange for limited relief.
timeline.problem_solved: Stopping program growth while a comprehensive deal was negotiated.
timeline.did_it_survive: Yes, until superseded by JCPOA implementation in January 2016.

timeline.name: Netanyahu addresses Congress against the Iran deal
timeline.line: Netanyahu lobbies Congress directly against the Obama administration's Iran negotiations
timeline.description: Invited by the House Speaker without White House coordination, Netanyahu argued the emerging deal would pave Iran's path to a bomb. Congress passed the Iran Nuclear Agreement Review Act (P.L. 114-17) in May, but a resolution of disapproval failed.
timeline.immediate_effect: Open rift between the Israeli and US governments.
timeline.long_term_effect: Made the Iran deal a partisan issue in the US, easing its 2018 abandonment.

timeline.name: Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action
timeline.line: JCPOA caps enrichment for sanctions relief; endorsed by UNSCR 2231
timeline.description: Iran accepted limits on enrichment and stockpiles with IAEA verification in exchange for lifting nuclear-related sanctions.
timeline.problem_solved: Iranian breakout time under a year.
timeline.did_it_survive: The US withdrew in May 2018; Iran exceeded the limits from 2019 and had enriched to 60 percent by 2021; the deal was moribund by 2025.

timeline.name: US-Israel Memorandum of Understanding on security assistance (FY2019-2028)
timeline.line: US commits $38 billion in military aid to Israel over ten years
timeline.description: Third ten-year MOU: $33 billion in Foreign Military Financing and $5 billion for missile defense, FY2019-FY2028. It is an executive understanding, not a treaty; Congress appropriates annually.
timeline.problem_solved: Predictable support for Israel's qualitative military edge after the Iran nuclear deal dispute.
timeline.did_it_survive: In force; supplemented by emergency appropriations during the 2023-25 war; negotiation of a successor MOU is pending.

timeline.name: Israel reveals Iran's seized nuclear archive
timeline.line: Netanyahu presents documents taken from Tehran on Iran's pre-2003 weapons program, a week before the US exits the JCPOA
timeline.description: Israel said Mossad removed a large archive from a Tehran warehouse detailing the pre-2003 AMAD weapons effort. The material supported the IAEA's later questions about undeclared sites; Iran called it fabricated.
timeline.immediate_effect: Reinforced the US withdrawal decision announced on 8 May.
timeline.long_term_effect: Became the basis for IAEA investigations into undeclared locations that culminated in the 2025 non-compliance finding.

timeline.name: US withdraws from the JCPOA; 'maximum pressure'
timeline.line: US exits the deal and reimposes sanctions; the 2019 Gulf incidents follow within a year
timeline.description: The US reimposed and expanded sanctions, driving Iranian oil exports down sharply in 2019.
timeline.immediate_effect: Iranian economy contracted; Iran began exceeding JCPOA limits in 2019.
timeline.long_term_effect: The precedent Iranian negotiators cite for demanding guarantees against future US reversals.

timeline.name: The IRGC is designated a foreign terrorist organisation
timeline.line: For the first time the US designates part of another state's armed forces as a terrorist organisation
timeline.description: The designation reached the force that controls the Gulf littoral and much of Iran's economy; Iran responded by designating US Central Command as a terrorist organisation.
timeline.immediate_effect: Legal exposure for anyone dealing with IRGC-linked firms; a further step down the escalation ladder weeks before the tanker attacks.
timeline.long_term_effect: Removed most of the remaining distinction between sanctioning a government and sanctioning its army, and complicated every later negotiation.

timeline.name: US killing of Qasem Soleimani and Iran's missile response
timeline.line: US drone strike kills the Quds Force commander; Iran fires warned missile salvos at US bases and both stop
timeline.description: Case record for base rates; the event is documented in detail as event:2020_soleimani. Iran's 8 January strike on Al Asad and Erbil was preceded by warning via Iraq, caused brain injuries but no deaths, and the US did not respond.
timeline.immediate_effect: De-escalation within five days.
timeline.long_term_effect: The anchor case for calibrated Iranian retaliation after a leadership killing.

timeline.name: Abraham Accords signed at the White House
timeline.line: Israel normalizes relations with the UAE and Bahrain, formalizing an Israel-Gulf alignment against Iran
timeline.description: The Abraham Accords Declaration and the accompanying Israel-UAE agreement and Israel-Bahrain declaration were signed at the White House on 15 September 2020, negotiated on the US side by a team led by presidential adviser Jared Kushner. Morocco and Sudan followed under separate arrangements.
timeline.immediate_effect: Open diplomatic, intelligence and commercial relations between Israel and two Gulf states for the first time since 1994.
timeline.long_term_effect: Created the regional structure Iran now reads as encirclement, and the political logic of Israeli-Gulf air and missile defence cooperation that was visible when Iranian salvoes crossed the region in 2024. It also decoupled Gulf normalization from any Palestinian settlement, which is the part of the accords that remains contested.

timeline.name: Killing of Mohsen Fakhrizadeh
timeline.line: Iran's top nuclear weapons scientist is killed near Tehran; vowed revenge does not materialize militarily
timeline.description: The head of the former AMAD program was killed in Absard; Iran blamed Israel, which did not confirm. Iran responded through its nuclear program: the Majlis passed a law in December 2020 mandating 20 percent enrichment and curbs on inspections.
timeline.immediate_effect: No military retaliation; nuclear escalation instead.
timeline.long_term_effect: Shows Iran can answer covert attacks by expanding the program rather than by force.

timeline.name: Israel moved into US Central Command
timeline.line: Pentagon moves Israel from European Command to Central Command after the Abraham Accords
timeline.description: The Unified Command Plan change placed Israel in the same US command as the Gulf states, formally completed later in 2021.
timeline.immediate_effect: Enabled routine planning between Israel, the US and Arab partners.
timeline.long_term_effect: The structure through which the US coordinated regional interception of Iran's April and October 2024 salvos.

timeline.name: Natanz sabotage; Iran begins 60 percent enrichment
timeline.line: An explosion knocks out power at Natanz during US-Iran talks; Iran answers by enriching to 60 percent
timeline.description: Iran blamed Israel for an explosion that cut power to Natanz centrifuges on 11 April 2021; two days later it announced enrichment to 60 percent, which the IAEA confirmed.
timeline.immediate_effect: Largest jump in enrichment level since the JCPOA.
timeline.long_term_effect: 60 percent material, a short technical step from weapons grade, became the core of every later breakout estimate.

timeline.name: The Houthi Red Sea campaign reroutes world shipping
timeline.line: A non-state armed group does to the Red Sea what Iran has never done to Hormuz
timeline.description: Beginning with the seizure of the Galaxy Leader in November 2023, Houthi missile and drone attacks on shipping caused most container lines to route around the Cape of Good Hope. The US announced Operation Prosperity Guardian in December 2023, and US and UK strikes followed in January 2024; traffic did not recover.
timeline.immediate_effect: War-risk premiums multiplied and Suez transits fell sharply for months.
timeline.long_term_effect: The most important comparison case in this file: it shows that durable chokepoint disruption is achievable with cheap weapons and does not require closing anything, and that escorts and strikes did not restore traffic. It also shows the limits of attributing an Iran-aligned actor's decisions to Tehran.

timeline.name: Tower 22 attack and US strikes on IRGC-linked targets
timeline.line: Drone attack by Iran-backed militia kills three US soldiers in Jordan; US hits Iraq and Syria, not Iran
timeline.description: US strikes on 2 February 2024 hit more than 85 targets used by the IRGC Quds Force and affiliated militias in Iraq and Syria. The US deliberately avoided Iranian territory; militia attacks on US forces largely stopped afterwards.
timeline.immediate_effect: Pause in militia attacks on US bases.
timeline.long_term_effect: Evidence for the US preference, before 2025, to punish Iran's partners rather than Iran.

timeline.name: Israeli strike on Iran's Damascus consulate and Iran's first direct attack
timeline.line: Israel kills IRGC generals in Damascus; Iran answers with some 300 drones and missiles, Israel with a limited strike near Isfahan
timeline.description: The 1 April strike killed IRGC Brigadier General Mohammad Reza Zahedi. Iran's 13-14 April salvo was telegraphed and largely intercepted with US, UK, French and Jordanian help; Israel's 19 April response hit an air-defense radar near Isfahan and both sides stopped.
timeline.immediate_effect: Shadow war became direct but bounded.
timeline.long_term_effect: Crossed the taboo on direct Iranian strikes on Israel.

timeline.name: First direct Iran-Israel strikes
timeline.line: Iran fires drones and missiles at Israel in April and October 2024; Israel strikes Iranian air defenses
timeline.description: After Israel struck Iran's consulate in Damascus on 1 April, Iran launched roughly 300 drones and missiles on 13-14 April, mostly intercepted with US and allied help; a second, larger ballistic strike followed on 1 October after the killing of Hezbollah's leader; Israel struck Iranian air defenses and missile production on 26 October.
timeline.immediate_effect: The shadow war became direct; the strait was not affected.
timeline.long_term_effect: Set the escalation ladder that the June 2025 war climbed.

timeline.name: Killing of Haniyeh in Tehran and Nasrallah in Beirut; Iran's October salvo
timeline.line: Hamas leader killed in an Iranian guesthouse; after Nasrallah's killing Iran fires about 180 ballistic missiles; Israel strikes Iran
timeline.description: Ismail Haniyeh was killed in Tehran on 31 July 2024 after the president's inauguration; Iran delayed retaliation for two months. After Israel killed Hezbollah's Hassan Nasrallah on 27 September, Iran fired a large ballistic salvo on 1 October; Israel struck Iranian air defenses and missile production on 26 October. Israel publicly acknowledged the Haniyeh killing in December 2024.
timeline.immediate_effect: Iran's air defenses degraded; exchange paused.
timeline.long_term_effect: Showed delayed, larger retaliation and left Iran exposed for the June 2025 campaign.

timeline.name: Fall of the Assad government in Syria
timeline.line: Rebel offensive topples Assad, cutting Iran's land route to Hezbollah
timeline.description: An 11-day offensive led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham took Damascus; Iran and a weakened Hezbollah did not intervene effectively.
timeline.immediate_effect: Iran lost its only state ally in the Arab world and its supply corridor to Lebanon.
timeline.long_term_effect: With Hezbollah degraded, removed the forward deterrent that had made striking Iran costly for Israel.

timeline.name: NSPM-2 restores maximum pressure
timeline.line: Trump's second-term memorandum orders maximum economic pressure and denial of 'all paths to a nuclear weapon'
timeline.description: The memorandum directed Treasury to sanction all persons evidenced to be violating Iran sanctions and aimed to drive Iranian oil exports toward zero, while leaving room for talks.
timeline.immediate_effect: Enforcement against oil shipments and Chinese buyers intensified.
timeline.long_term_effect: Paired with an offer of talks, it set the pressure-plus-deadline sequence that ended in strikes in June 2025.

timeline.name: US-Iran talks mediated by Oman
timeline.line: Highest-level US-Iran nuclear talks since 2018 open in Muscat; they stall over enrichment
timeline.description: Five rounds between US envoy Steve Witkoff and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, hosted or mediated by Oman, ran from April to late May 2025. The US moved toward demanding zero enrichment; Iran refused. A sixth round scheduled for mid-June was overtaken by Israel's strikes.
timeline.immediate_effect: No agreement.
timeline.long_term_effect: Iran's reading that the talks masked a strike plan hardened its later demand for guarantees.

timeline.name: IAEA Board finds Iran in non-compliance for the first time in two decades
timeline.line: IAEA Board declares Iran non-compliant a day before Israel's strikes
timeline.description: Resolution GOV/2025/38, tabled by the E3 and the US, passed 25-2 with 7 abstentions, citing Iran's failure to explain uranium traces at undeclared locations. Iran announced a new enrichment site in response.
timeline.immediate_effect: Iran announced expansion; Israel struck the next day.
timeline.long_term_effect: Provided the legal predicate the E3 later used for snapback, and the Israeli government cited it when launching strikes.

timeline.name: June 2025 Israel-Iran war and Majlis closure vote
timeline.line: Israel and then the US strike Iran's nuclear sites; parliament votes to close Hormuz; the strait stays open and a ceasefire follows
timeline.description: Israel opened a campaign against Iranian nuclear and military targets on 13 June; the US struck Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan on 22 June; Iran's parliament voted the same day to close the strait, a decision left to the Supreme National Security Council and not executed; Iran fired a telegraphed salvo at Al Udeid on 23 June; a ceasefire took hold on 24 June.
timeline.immediate_effect: Twelve-day war; oil rose then fell back when the strait stayed open.
timeline.long_term_effect: Even under direct attack on its nuclear program, Iran did not close the strait; the strongest data point yet for the not_implemented pattern, and also a data point for how far escalation can go without closure. Superseded in March 2026, when Iran did block the strait and then licensed passage through it: see case:2026_hormuz_closure_permit_regime. The 2025 case now reads as the last data point of the old pattern rather than as proof of it.

timeline.name: Israeli and US strikes on Iran's nuclear program, June 2025
timeline.line: Israel strikes Iran for twelve days; US bombers hit Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan; ceasefire on 24 June
timeline.description: Base-rate record of the preventive dimension of the June 2025 war (the Hormuz dimension is case:2025_june_war). Israel's campaign killed senior commanders and nuclear scientists and struck enrichment and missile sites; the US struck the three main nuclear sites on 22 June; Iran answered with missile barrages on Israel and a telegraphed salvo at Al Udeid.
timeline.immediate_effect: Ceasefire after twelve days; damage to the program disputed.
timeline.long_term_effect: The first time the US itself bombed Iran's nuclear program; Iran then curtailed IAEA access, leaving the program's status unverifiable.

timeline.name: Iran suspends cooperation with the IAEA
timeline.line: After the strikes, Iran's parliament and president suspend cooperation with IAEA inspectors
timeline.description: A law passed by the Majlis and promulgated in early July 2025 made inspector access subject to Supreme National Security Council approval; inspectors left Iran. Partial arrangements discussed with the IAEA later in 2025 did not restore routine verification.
timeline.immediate_effect: Loss of continuity of knowledge on the enriched stockpile.
timeline.long_term_effect: Uncertainty about the 60 percent stockpile became a driver of the 2026 war and a core MOU issue.

timeline.name: E3 snapback reimposes UN sanctions
timeline.line: Britain, France and Germany trigger snapback; pre-2016 UN sanctions return
timeline.description: The E3 notified the Security Council on 28 August 2025 of Iran's significant non-performance; after a Russia-China extension resolution failed, the UN sanctions lifted in 2016 were reinstated at the end of 27 September 2025 (New York time). Iran, Russia and China reject their validity.
timeline.immediate_effect: EU and UK reimposed their own measures within days.
timeline.long_term_effect: Ended the JCPOA's legal architecture and removed the European bridge between Washington and Tehran.

timeline.name: DOJ publishes the Epstein files under the Transparency Act
timeline.line: Roughly 3.5 million pages released; no document establishes an intelligence relationship
timeline.description: Under the Epstein Files Transparency Act signed on 19 November 2025, the Department of Justice published over 3 million additional pages - about 3.5 million with prior releases - plus more than 2,000 videos and 180,000 images, stating that notable individuals and politicians were not redacted and that the production included material falsely submitted to the FBI.
timeline.immediate_effect: Superseded the July 2025 memorandum's position that no further disclosure was warranted.
timeline.long_term_effect: Gives the claim about Epstein and intelligence services a testable record for the first time. As of this build, nothing in that record establishes such a relationship. This is recorded so the desk stops arguing the claim from rumour in either direction.

timeline.name: US executive order imposing tariffs on buyers of Iranian goods
timeline.line: Washington threatens tariffs on any country that buys Iranian goods, three weeks before the war
timeline.description: The order reaffirmed the national emergency on Iran and authorized additional tariffs on imports from countries that directly or indirectly buy Iranian goods or services.
timeline.immediate_effect: Raised costs for Iran's remaining buyers.
timeline.long_term_effect: Extended the sanctions toolkit from finance into trade policy.

timeline.name: US-Israeli war on Iran (Operation Epic Fury / Roaring Lion)
timeline.line: US and Israel launch a war on Iran that kills Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei; Iran strikes Israel and Gulf states hosting US forces
timeline.description: Joint strikes began on 28 February 2026 against nuclear, missile and command targets and killed Ali Khamenei and senior officials. Iran and allied militias struck Israel and US-hosting Gulf states including Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE; Hezbollah opened fire from Lebanon. A Pakistan-mediated ceasefire took effect on 8 April but was repeatedly violated. Sources disagree on when major combat ended.
timeline.immediate_effect: Leadership succession in wartime; Gulf energy and shipping disrupted.
timeline.long_term_effect: Broke the pre-2025 pattern in which the US avoided direct war with Iran; the war ran from a preventive strike to regime decapitation, beyond the Osirak or al-Kibar template.

timeline.name: Iran blocks Hormuz and imposes a permit-and-toll regime
timeline.line: For the first time Iran actually closes the strait, then runs it through a permit and toll authority
timeline.description: During the war Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz (late March 2026 per available accounts) and asserted authority over it. In early May it launched a 'Persian Gulf Strait Authority' requiring vessel declarations and fees before IRGC-coordinated transit. The June MOU promised 60 days of toll-free passage; at the August deadline traffic remained a small fraction of prewar levels and Iran insisted on charging fees.
timeline.immediate_effect: Collapse of commercial transits; US counter-blockade of Iranian ports reported from April.
timeline.long_term_effect: The first case in the record of an executed, sustained Hormuz disruption; it breaks the 'threat not closure' pattern once the regime itself was under direct attack.

timeline.name: Mojtaba Khamenei becomes Supreme Leader
timeline.line: Assembly of Experts names Ali Khamenei's son Supreme Leader after a wartime interim council
timeline.description: An interim council of the president, the chief justice and Ayatollah Alireza Arafi held authority from 1 March; the Assembly of Experts voted on 8 March and the choice was announced on 9 March. Opposition-aligned media reported IRGC pressure on members; that account is contested.
timeline.immediate_effect: Continuity of the Islamic Republic; no regime change.
timeline.long_term_effect: Hereditary-looking succession under war conditions; the balance between the new Leader and the IRGC is the key unknown for Iranian decision-making.

timeline.name: Pakistan-mediated ceasefire and Islamabad talks
timeline.line: A two-week ceasefire trades a halt to strikes for reopening Hormuz; talks in Islamabad fail
timeline.description: The US and Israel agreed to pause attacks and Iran to allow coordinated passage through the strait for two weeks. Direct talks in Islamabad on 11-12 April between Vice President JD Vance and Majlis speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf did not produce a deal; reported US naval blockade of Iran followed, and the truce was violated repeatedly but extended.
timeline.immediate_effect: Reduced but did not end fighting.
timeline.long_term_effect: Made Pakistan, not Oman or Qatar, the principal channel in the war's diplomacy.

timeline.name: US-Iran Memorandum of Understanding of 17 June 2026
timeline.line: 14-point MOU halts hostilities and sets a 60-day window for a final deal on Hormuz, the nuclear program and sanctions
timeline.description: The published text declares a permanent end to military operations on all fronts including Lebanon, 60 days of toll-free passage through Hormuz with demining, downblending of enriched material under IAEA supervision, oil-sale waivers, a negotiation window of 60 days extendable by consent, and a requirement that a final deal be endorsed by a binding Security Council resolution. Sources disagree on where it was signed (Islamabad or Versailles).
timeline.problem_solved: Stopping the war and reopening the strait while deferring enrichment, missiles and sanctions to a final agreement.
timeline.did_it_survive: Partially: the 60-day window expired on 17 August 2026 without a final deal, the US rejected an extension, and the Hormuz provisions were not implemented as written; the ceasefire itself remained fragile but broadly in place.

timeline.name: MOU deadline lapses; US launches 'Operation Economic Outcast'
timeline.line: The 60-day window ends with no deal; a week later Washington announces a campaign to cut Iran's remaining economic lifelines
timeline.description: At the 17 August deadline the sides were deadlocked over control of Hormuz and nuclear talks had barely begun; Trump rejected an extension. On 24 August the White House announced 'Operation Economic Outcast' to isolate Iran financially.
timeline.immediate_effect: Return to maximum pressure without a resumption of full-scale war as of mid-September 2026.
timeline.long_term_effect: Too recent to judge.

lessons.name: Israel: prevent hostile states from acquiring nuclear capability, by force if necessary ('Begin Doctrine')
lessons.description: The label is scholarly and journalistic shorthand; its content rests on documented statements: the Begin government's 1981 statement after Osirak and IDF Chief of Staff Eisenkot's 2018 statement that Israel will not accept a capability that threatens its existence. No single public Israeli doctrine document codifies it.

lessons.name: Preventive strikes delay programs but can convert them into covert weapons drives
lessons.description: Braut-Hegghammer's archival work on Iraq finds Osirak intensified Saddam's pursuit of a bomb. Applying this to Iran after 2025-26 is an inference: Iran's suspension of IAEA cooperation is consistent with it, but the program's actual state is unverified.

lessons.name: Iran: disarmament invites regime change (the Libya lesson)
lessons.description: Ali Khamenei said in March 2011 that Gaddafi had packed up his nuclear program and handed it to the West, and that Libya lost everything; Iranian hardliners repeated the warning during the 2025 talks. The 2003 Iraq invasion is read the same way. That this lesson drives Iranian refusal of zero enrichment is a well-supported interpretation, not a published doctrine.

lessons.name: Iran: US agreements can be reversed by the next administration, so demand guarantees
lessons.description: Iranian negotiators have cited the 2018 US exit from the JCPOA ever since. The June 2026 MOU's requirement that a final deal be endorsed by a binding Security Council resolution is documentary evidence of the demand; the underlying lesson is interpretation.

lessons.name: Pressure without a verification regime has grown Iran's program and shrunk what outsiders know about it
lessons.description: Inference from the sequence 2018-2025: Iran went from JCPOA caps to 60 percent enrichment and a stockpile above 400 kg under maximum pressure, and each escalation (sabotage, strikes) was followed by reduced IAEA access. Counter-view: without pressure and strikes Iran might have gone further; the counterfactual cannot be observed.

lessons.name: The paper often precedes the policy, and the authors often precede themselves into office
lessons.description: On this file the sequence paper-then-post is documented more than once: the 1996 IASPS study group named removing Saddam Hussein as an objective and three of its participants held or advised US policy offices from 2001; the 2009 Brookings volume spelled out the offer-refusal-strike sequence a decade and a half before it was visible in practice. The standard reading in the literature is that such papers reveal a policy community's preferences and supply the vocabulary, not that they cause decisions. Both halves matter: reading the papers tells you what a camp will propose when a window opens; it does not tell you that the window was opened for them.
lessons.caveat: The competing causal reading - that 9/11, Iranian behaviour and the IAEA record drove these decisions and the papers merely anticipated them - is held by serious scholarship and is not refuted by the personnel overlap.

lessons.name: Grade a principal's threat claim against that principal's own dated record
lessons.description: A single warning cannot be scored. A thirty-year series can. Netanyahu's Iran estimates run from 1992 ('three to five years'), through the 1995 book, the 2012 UN red line ('by next spring, at most by next summer'), to 2015 and 2025; his 2002 testimony to Congress on Iraq made the same structure of claim and the Iraq Survey Group found no active programme. The inference is methodological, not political: when a principal makes the same prediction for decades, the base rate of that principal's horizons is evidence, and it cuts both ways - Iran's programme did grow, and the IAEA did find non-compliance twice, so being early is not the same as being wrong.
lessons.caveat: ANALYST_INFERENCE, not doctrine. Applying it only to one principal would be the bias it is meant to prevent; the same test applies to Iranian, US and European claims in this graph.

lessons.name: Registry facts are evidence of interest, never of causation
lessons.description: FEC Schedule A, Senate LDA filings and FARA registrations establish who paid whom, how much and when. They do not establish that a policy followed from it. On this file the disclosed money runs in both directions - hundreds of millions in itemized contributions to committees aligned with the pressure camp, and named foundation funding behind the restraint camp - and the largest single organized constituency by membership is evangelical rather than Jewish. The desk records the documented interest of named actors and grades the causal claim separately, case by case, which is also what keeps the record usable by people who disagree about the conclusion.
lessons.caveat: Contributions to multi-issue political committees are not earmarked to any foreign-policy question. Treat the totals as a map of interest, not as a mechanism.

tendencies.name: Iran retaliates in ways that are visible, deniable or telegraphed, and stop short of war with the US
contradicting: The 1984-88 Tanker War escalated to direct US-Iran naval combat; the 2019 Abqaiq attack, if Iranian, was a major unclaimed strike on a US partner; the October 2024 salvo was larger and less telegraphed than April's.

The 2026 war broke the pattern at both ends: Iran's retaliation for the strikes that killed Ali Khamenei included attacks on Gulf states hosting US forces and an actual blockade of the strait, neither of which is calibrated in the sense the earlier cases were.
current_evidence: The June 2025 Al Udeid strike was announced in advance through Qatar and caused no casualties.
Under Mojtaba Khamenei the record is six months long and wartime; the April 2026 ceasefire and the June MOU were accepted while the toll regime was kept in place.
tendencies.caveat: Calibration held while the regime's survival was not at stake and while Ali Khamenei was making the decisions. Both conditions failed in 2026. Any use of this tendency now has to say which leadership it describes.

tendencies.name: The US punishes Iran's partners and squeezes its economy but avoids direct war with Iran itself
current_evidence: The US bombed Iran's nuclear sites in June 2025 and went to war with Iran in February 2026; after the MOU lapsed in August 2026 it returned to economic pressure rather than resuming full-scale strikes.
tendencies.caveat: Held for four decades across administrations of both parties, then broke twice in nine months under one president. Whether the break is a new pattern or a Trump-specific deviation cannot be settled from the record; treat as a weakened prior.

tendencies.name: Israel uses force to stop hostile states from approaching nuclear capability
contradicting: Israel did not strike Iran's program for more than two decades after it was revealed in 2002, choosing sabotage, assassinations and lobbying (event:2015_netanyahu_congress) while Iran reached 60 percent enrichment.
Against Fordow in 2025 Israel depended on US bombers, so its preventive action against Iran has not been independent.
current_evidence: Israel opened the June 2025 campaign and joined the February 2026 war.
tendencies.caveat: The tendency acts when Israel judges a program close and a strike feasible; against dispersed, hardened Iranian sites feasibility has depended on US participation, so Israeli preference alone is a poor predictor of timing.

tendencies.name: Iran stays a threshold state: builds capability, does not test or openly weaponize
current_evidence: In the June 2026 MOU Iran reaffirmed it will not acquire nuclear weapons and agreed in principle to downblend enriched material, but no IAEA verification of the stockpile has been reported since mid-2025.
tendencies.caveat: The pre-2003 archive shows a weapons program existed; the pattern of restraint was observed under Ali Khamenei and under a verification regime that no longer operates. A new Leader after a decapitation war could draw the opposite lesson.

tendencies.name: Israel takes the Iran argument to the US Congress and public when the US executive diverges
current_evidence: The 2015 address to a joint meeting of Congress was arranged with Speaker Boehner without prior notice to the White House, during an executive-led negotiation; the 2018 nuclear-archive presentation was staged in English days before a US decision.
AIPAC's 2026 LDA filings list Foreign Relations, Defense and Budget/Appropriations as its issue areas, which is where Iran sanctions legislation lives.
tendencies.caveat: The counter-cases are strong and recent. The largest instruments of the relationship - the 2016 security-assistance MOU, the 2021 move of Israel into CENTCOM, the 2018 withdrawal itself - were executive acts obtained through the executive, and the 2015 congressional campaign failed to stop the deal. The tendency describes a fallback channel used when the executive diverges, not the main one, and it should never be stated as though Congress substitutes for the White House on this file.

path_dependencies.name: From the 2018 JCPOA exit to the 2026 war

chain.step: 2018: US leaves the JCPOA and reimposes sanctions
2019-2021: Iran exceeds limits; after the Natanz sabotage it enriches to 60 percent
2025: maximum pressure plus talks; IAEA non-compliance finding
June 2025: Israeli and US strikes; Iran suspends IAEA cooperation; E3 snapback
February 2026: war, Khamenei killed; Hormuz closed
June-August 2026: MOU, then deadline lapses without a final deal
Current constraint: no verification of the stockpile, a new Leader, Hormuz under an Iranian toll regime, and a US return to economic pressure

path_dependencies.description: Each arrow is a hypothesis about causation. The documents and dates are established; how much each step caused the next, and what would have happened without the 2018 exit, is an assessment.

path_dependencies.name: From Hezbollah's founding to Iran's exposure to direct attack

chain.step: 1982: IRGC helps create Hezbollah on Israel's border
2003-2023: Iran builds a partner network across Iraq, Syria, Yemen and Gaza as forward deterrence
October 2023: Hamas attack triggers multi-front war
2024: Hezbollah's leadership killed; Assad falls
Current constraint: Iran's deterrent shifted from partners to its own missiles and to Hormuz, which it then used

path_dependencies.description: Each arrow is a hypothesis. That forward deterrence restrained Israeli strikes on Iran before 2024 is a common interpretation, not a documented Israeli decision record.

path_dependencies.name: From the 1996 paper to the 2026 strikes: the documented steps and the assessed arrows

chain.step: 1996: an IASPS study group led by Perle, with Feith and the Wurmsers, publishes 'A Clean Break', naming the removal of Saddam Hussein as a means of rolling back Syria and naming Hezbollah, Syria and Iran as the agents of aggression in Lebanon (DOCUMENTED: the text)
2001-2005: Perle chairs the Defense Policy Board, Feith is Under Secretary of Defense for Policy, Wurmser advises in the administration (DOCUMENTED: the appointments)
2003: the United States invades Iraq and removes Saddam Hussein (DOCUMENTED: the event; ASSESSED and contested: that the 1996 advocacy contributed to it)

2003-2011: Iraq's removal takes out Iran's strongest regional counterweight and Iran's influence in Baghdad and Beirut grows - the outcome opposite to the one the paper's sponsors wanted (DOCUMENTED: the regional result; ASSESSED: the causal weight)
2009: a Brookings volume sets out an options menu including the sequence in which a refused offer creates the international context for a strike (DOCUMENTED: the text; NO CLAIM of influence)
2018: the United States leaves the JCPOA and restores maximum pressure (DOCUMENTED)

2025-2026: offer through Oman, deadline, strikes on the nuclear programme, then war, then a lapsed Memorandum and Operation Economic Outcast (DOCUMENTED: the sequence; ASSESSED: that it followed anyone's script)
Current constraint: Iran's programme is less observed than at any point since 2003, the leadership has changed, and the US instruments that remain are economic (ASSESSED)

path_dependencies.description: Every arrow here is a hypothesis and each step is labelled DOCUMENTED or ASSESSED so the two are never merged. The competing causal reading - that 9/11, the IAEA's findings and Iran's own conduct drove each decision and the papers merely anticipated the logic - is not refuted by anything in this chain, and the 2003-2011 step is the strongest evidence against treating the chain as a plan being executed: it produced the opposite of what its advocates sought.

narratives.name: Iran: a century of foreign interference justifies resistance and self-reliance
narratives.historical_event: 1953 coup; 1980-88 war; sanctions
narratives.modern_interpretation: The Islamic Republic frames its foreign policy as resistance to US and Israeli domination. The 1953 coup is documented; the claim that current US policy continues it is a political interpretation.

narratives.name: US: Iran as a hostage-taking, terror-sponsoring regime since 1979
narratives.historical_event: 1979-81 embassy seizure; 1983 Beirut bombings
narratives.modern_interpretation: Frames US policy across administrations and constrains any president's room to normalize relations. The events are documented; the framing is a domestic political narrative.

narratives.name: Israel: a nuclear Iran is an existential threat, framed through the Holocaust
narratives.historical_event: The Holocaust; Iranian leaders' repeated calls for Israel's elimination since 1979; Iran's pre-2003 weapons work
narratives.modern_interpretation: Netanyahu has framed Iran's program for decades as a threat of a second Holocaust and argued that Israel cannot rely on others to stop it. The underlying statements and archive are documented; the inference that deterrence could not work against a nuclear Iran is a contested strategic judgment.
used_in: statements launching the June 2025 and February 2026 operations

narratives.name: The argument about domestic influence on US Iran policy
narratives.historical_event: A documented record: AIPAC's LDA filings ($844,410 and $810,990 in the first two quarters of 2026, issue areas including Foreign Relations and Defense); itemized FEC contributions by individual donors running into the hundreds of millions per cycle; a 1996 strategy paper written by people who later held US policy offices; a 2015 address to Congress arranged around a sitting president; and, on the other side, named foundation funding for restraint-oriented institutes and the largest pro-Israel membership organization in the US being an evangelical one.
narratives.modern_interpretation: One reading, argued at book length by Mearsheimer and Walt in 2007, holds that a loose coalition of organizations, donors and officials has pushed US Middle East policy away from what a plain national-interest calculation would produce, and points to the 2018 withdrawal from an agreement the IAEA was certifying as the case a pure-interest account cannot explain. The competing reading holds that US policy tracks genuine strategic disagreement about a sunsetted deal, the electoral weight of a large evangelical constituency, and Iranian conduct - and that the influence thesis understates all three while flattening many distinct actors into one agent. Both readings are held by serious people and neither is settled by the registry record, which shows interest rather than mechanism.
used_in: Iranian and Russian state media, which use the stronger version of the first reading as evidence that American policy is not American
Academic and think-tank argument in Washington
narratives.caveat: The desk records named actors with documented interests and their sources, whichever side they cut for. It does not record, and will not carry, the collective claim that a group as such controls an outcome: that is not a graph fact, it is a proposition to be graded on the read, and the graph exists to make that grading checkable.

narratives.name: Epstein and the intelligence-services claim
narratives.historical_event: Jeffrey Epstein's 2007-08 federal non-prosecution agreement and 2008 Florida state plea, his 2019 federal charges and death in custody on 10 August 2019, his documented social and financial contact with politicians and former officials in several countries, and the subsequent government releases.
narratives.modern_interpretation: One reading holds that Epstein worked for or was protected by an intelligence service - most often US or Israeli - and that this explains the 2008 agreement and the access; it rests largely on a 2019 press report of an unrecorded remark attributed to the prosecutor who signed that agreement, a remark he did not confirm publicly. The competing reading holds that the leniency is fully explained by wealth, counsel and prosecutorial discretion, and that the intelligence story is a conspiracy frame that has been used to attach a foreign government to an American scandal. What the released record shows: the Department of Justice and FBI review published in July 2025 found no incriminating client list, no credible evidence that Epstein blackmailed prominent individuals, and no evidence supporting an investigation of uncharged third parties; the Department then published roughly 3.5 million pages by 30 January 2026 under a statute passed to force disclosure. No released document establishes a relationship with any intelligence service.
used_in: US domestic politics across the spectrum
Antisemitic and anti-Israel propaganda, where the claim is used to assert covert foreign control
Arguments about prosecutorial capture and elite impunity that do not depend on the intelligence claim at all
narratives.caveat: Recorded as a NARRATIVE and never as an EVENT, because there is no settled record. The releases are evidence about what the government collected, not proof about what was never written down; absence of a document is not proof of absence. The desk's rule here: state what the released record shows, name the unverified sub-claim as unverified, and do not let either the rumour or the denial travel as a fact.

narratives.name: The 'nuclear fatwa'
narratives.historical_event: An oral position attributed to Khamenei in October 2003 forbidding weapons of mass destruction; cited by Iran at the IAEA in Vienna in August 2005; and a 2010 message to a Tehran disarmament conference whose closing passage is the text posted in the fatwa section of khamenei.ir.
narratives.modern_interpretation: Iran presents it as a binding religious ruling that settles the question of intent, and Western negotiators including President Obama cited it publicly as a route to compromise. Critics answer that no written fatwa existed when it was first claimed, that Khamenei's authority to issue one is itself disputed, that the text addresses use rather than production, and that a fatwa can be revised as conditions change - pointing to Khamenei's own 2011 remarks that Libya erred in surrendering its programme. After the 2025 and 2026 strikes and the July 2025 suspension of IAEA cooperation, Iranian officials and clerics have been quoted on both sides of whether it still binds.
used_in: Iranian diplomacy at the IAEA and the UN
US arguments for and against a negotiated ceiling on enrichment
Israeli arguments that Iranian declarations of intent are worthless
narratives.caveat: A declaration of intent is not a capability constraint either way. Whether the fatwa exists as a text does not settle what Iran will do, and treating the dispute over the text as the substance of the nuclear question is a category error both camps make.

Iran seizes fifteen Royal Navy personnel
IRGC fast boats swarm US warships in the strait
Closure threats during the 2011-12 sanctions escalation
Iran seizes the Maersk Tigris in the strait
Ten US sailors detained at Farsi Island
Closure threats after the US withdrawal from the nuclear deal
2019 tanker attacks, drone shoot-down and seizures
Iran seizes two Greek tankers after a cargo confiscation
2023 tanker seizures (Advantage Sweet, Niovi)
Iran seizes the St Nikolas and the MSC Aries
June 2025 Israel-Iran war and Majlis closure vote

pooled.note: n=13; pooling moves it 38% toward the parent distribution over 101 classed cases.

hormuz_disruption.selection_note: Cases are episodes in which Iran threatened, attacked, boarded or seized shipping or naval personnel in or near the Strait of Hormuz, or acted to control passage through it. Coding: 'not_implemented' means a closure threat was made and not acted on; 'limited_conflict' means attacks or seizures occurred without closure; 'de_escalation' means an incident ended within days with the people or ship returned and no further action; 'prolonged_standoff' is used for the 2026 blockade and permit regime, which is still running. The set is assembled from publicised incidents, so it over-represents episodes that governments wanted known and under-represents routine harassment, near-misses and the many US cargo confiscations that drew no Iranian response. The 1984-88 Tanker War is counted once although it contains hundreds of attacks, which understates how violent that period was relative to the single-incident cases. Most importantly, the set is not a sample of independent draws: eleven of the cases fall under Ali Khamenei's leadership and one under his successor's, and the first executed disruption in the whole record came in 2026, after the strikes on Iran's nuclear programme and his death. A base rate built on the pre-2026 cases would have said closure does not happen; it happened. Use the distribution as a prior about peacetime pressure and discard it for wartime.

cases.name: Israeli strike on Iraq's Osirak reactor (Operation Opera)
Operation Desert Fox against Iraq's WMD programs
Israeli strike on Syria's al-Kibar reactor
Israeli and US strikes on Iran's nuclear program, June 2025
US-Israeli war on Iran (Operation Epic Fury / Roaring Lion)

pooled.note: n=5 is below the low-n floor of 8: the pooled figure is 62% the parent class, not this class. Publish the interval, name n, and say the reference class is thin.

preventive_strike_nuclear_program.selection_note: Cases are uses of military force by one state against another state's nuclear or WMD program outside an already-running war: Osirak 1981, Desert Fox 1998, al-Kibar 2007, June 2025, February 2026. The 2003 Iraq invasion is recorded as an event, not a case, because WMD was one of several war aims. Strikes inside ongoing wars (Iran on Osirak in 1980, Coalition strikes in 1991) and covert sabotage or assassinations are excluded, so the set overweights overt, attributable action. 'outcome' codes the military aftermath of the strike, NOT whether the program ended. The 2025 and 2026 cases involve the same target and actors and are not independent draws; n is small.
preventive_strike_nuclear_program.note: only 5 comparable cases: use as a rough prior, not a percentage

Killing of Imad Mughniyeh in Damascus
Killings of Iranian nuclear scientists and the 2012 attacks on Israeli diplomats
US killing of Qasem Soleimani and Iran's missile response
Killing of Mohsen Fakhrizadeh
Israeli strike on Iran's Damascus consulate and Iran's first direct attack
Killing of Haniyeh in Tehran and Nasrallah in Beirut; Iran's October salvo

targeted_killing_retaliation.selection_note: Cases are killings of senior Iranian or Iran-aligned figures attributed to the US or Israel and coded by what Iran did in response: scientists 2010-12, Soleimani 2020, Fakhrizadeh 2020, Damascus consulate 2024, Haniyeh/Nasrallah 2024. The February 2026 killing of Ali Khamenei is excluded because it was part of a war already launched (see case:2026_epic_fury). Selection bias: only publicized killings are included, and all cases fall under Ali Khamenei's leadership, so the set describes his decision style, not his successor's.

links.continuity: India kept British India's UN membership, treaty obligations, capital, and most of the army and civil service structures.
links.discontinuity: Lost the Muslim-majority provinces to Pakistan; paramountcy over princely states lapsed and they had to accede separately.

links.continuity: Inherited part of the British Indian Army, civil service and legal system, and the Durand Line with Afghanistan.
links.discontinuity: A new state that had to apply for UN membership (admitted September 1947) and build a capital and institutions from scratch; it received a minority of military stores.

links.continuity: Bangladesh comprises the former East Pakistan (earlier East Bengal) and its population.
links.discontinuity: Secession by war; Bengali language nationalism replaced the religious basis of Pakistani identity. Pakistan continued as the same state in the west and recognized Bangladesh in 1974.

links.continuity: Ottoman land law (the 1858 Land Code) and religious personal-status courts carried into Mandate law, and from there into Israeli, Jordanian and PA legal systems.
links.discontinuity: Sovereignty lapsed under the Treaty of Lausanne; the Mandate was a League trust with a Jewish-national-home obligation the Ottoman state never had; borders were redrawn.

links.continuity: Section 11 of the 1948 Law and Administration Ordinance kept Mandate law in force unless changed; British emergency defence regulations are still used.
